title: Local orbit formula for characters
notes: The heading says \ru{без доказательства или противоречащих примеров}. Near the identity it proposes \(\chi(x)=p(x)^{-1/2}\int_\Omega e^{i\langle F,x\rangle}\beta(F)\) for irreducible representations of Lie groups.
statement: For a connected simply connected nilpotent Lie group, the irreducible unitary representation associated with a coadjoint orbit has distribution character equal, in exponential coordinates and with compatible Fourier conventions, to the Fourier transform of the canonical orbital measure. For compact connected groups the corresponding local formula uses the orbit through the highest weight plus \(\rho\), and the square root of the exponential Jacobian. Neither statement is an unrestricted formula for every irreducible representation of every Lie group.
reconstruction: The two precise proved settings replace the notebook's unrestricted scope. No general orbit-method conjecture is silently converted into a theorem.
fate: \citet[Introduction and the nilpotent and compact cases]{kirillov1968characters} develops the announced formula; the manuscript was received 18 October 1967 and published in 1968. The nilpotent orbit correspondence was already available in \citet{kirillov1962unitary}. The publication match is partial because the notebook suppresses the admissibility, normalization, and representation-class restrictions.
present_status: As of November 2026, these nilpotent and compact character formulas are established. The universal formulation in the notes is too broad to have a single affirmative status.

title: Distribution character and the missing trace
notes: For a finite-dimensional representation the notes give \(\chi(g)=\operatorname{tr}T(g)\). In the general case they write \(\langle\chi,\varphi\rangle=\int_G\varphi(g)T(g)\,dg\), adding that the latter already has a trace.
statement: For a representation for which \(T(\varphi)=\int_G\varphi(g)T(g)\,dg\) is trace class for every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(G)\), its distribution character is \(\Theta_T(\varphi)=\operatorname{tr}T(\varphi)\). The integral itself is an operator, not a scalar distribution value; trace-class admissibility is an additional hypothesis.
reconstruction: The trace-class condition and the outer trace are explicit editorial repairs.
fate: This is the character convention used in \citet[Introduction]{kirillov1968characters}. The notebook has omitted the outer trace while preserving an explanatory phrase that makes the intended correction clear.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Canonical form and measure on a coadjoint orbit
notes: The form \(\beta\) is said to be constructed from the structure constants; the final line mentions integrals of integral forms over cycles of the orbit.
statement: At \(F\in\mathfrak g^*\), the Kirillov form on the coadjoint orbit is \(\omega_F(\operatorname{ad}_X^*F,\operatorname{ad}_Y^*F)=\langle F,[X,Y]\rangle\), up to the sign convention for the coadjoint action. It is closed and nondegenerate. On an orbit of dimension \(2d\), the corresponding Liouville measure is a fixed Fourier-normalized multiple of \(\omega^d/d!\).
reconstruction: The symplectic formula makes precise the otherwise unspecified construction from structure constants; the sign and Fourier normalization are deliberately not inferred from the notebook.
fate: The canonical orbital measure is part of the framework in \citet[Introduction]{kirillov1968characters}, extending the earlier nilpotent setting of \citet{kirillov1962unitary}. The notebook's cycle phrase does not give a separate computable formula for \(\beta\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Integrality and the shifted compact orbit
notes: Only certain orbits satisfying integrality conditions are to occur. The rotation example selects \(\lambda=2n+1\).
statement: Prequantization of a symplectic orbit requires \([\omega/(2\pi)]\) to be integral. Equivariance under a specified group can impose a stronger lattice condition. In the compact character formula the orbit is shifted by \(\rho\); therefore an unshifted assertion that every integral orbit directly labels a character is insufficient. For \(SO(3)\), the representations have integral spin \(n\geq0\), while the character formula below contains \(2n+1\).
reconstruction: Prequantization, group equivariance, and the \(\rho\)-shift are separated here rather than merged into the ambiguous word integrality.
fate: \citet[compact-group discussion]{kirillov1968characters} supplies the compact character setting. The notes announce an integrality requirement but do not state which lattice or shift is intended.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Exponential Haar density for the rotation example
notes: The notebook visibly writes \(p(x)=\sin\tau/\tau\), without a square, and then applies \(p^{-1/2}\).
statement: If \(\tau\) denotes half the rotation angle, the exponential-coordinate Haar Jacobian, normalized at zero, is \(j(x)=(\sin\tau/\tau)^2\). If \(\theta\) is the full angle, it is \((\sin(\theta/2)/(\theta/2))^2\). Its square root, rather than the density itself, is \(\sin\tau/\tau\) near zero.
reconstruction: The half-angle convention is chosen to make the subsequent character formula consistent; the notebook does not explicitly specify this normalization.
fate: The determinant factor in the compact case of \citet{kirillov1968characters} and the elementary eigenvalues \(0,\pm 2i\tau\) of \(\operatorname{ad}_x\) identify the missing square. The displayed formula is faithfully transcribed, not an OCR mistake.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Fourier transform of the spherical orbital measure
notes: The notes give \((\delta_{S_\lambda})^\sim=\sin(\lambda\tau)/\tau\), then call \(\beta\) ordinary surface area.
statement: With Fourier kernel \(e^{i\langle F,x\rangle}\) and Euclidean area \(dS\) on the sphere of radius \(\lambda>0\), \(\int_{S_\lambda}e^{i\langle F,x\rangle}dS=4\pi\lambda\sin(\lambda|x|)/|x|\). The measure \(dS/(4\pi\lambda)\) gives the notebook's transform and has mass \(\lambda\).
reconstruction: The calculation is an editorial normalization check, not a new character theorem.
fate: This direct spherical-coordinate calculation fixes the normalization required by the compact orbit formula of \citet{kirillov1968characters}. The words ordinary surface cannot be read literally together with the displayed equality under this Fourier convention.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The irreducible characters of SO(3)
notes: The answer is \(\chi(x)=\sin(\lambda\tau)/\sin\tau\), for \(\lambda=2n+1\).
statement: For the irreducible \((2n+1)\)-dimensional representation of \(SO(3)\), a rotation through angle \(\theta\) has character \(\chi_n(\theta)=\sin((n+\tfrac12)\theta)/\sin(\theta/2)\), interpreted continuously at multiples of \(2\pi\). Setting \(\tau=\theta/2\) gives exactly the recorded expression and \(\chi_n(e)=2n+1\).
reconstruction: The parameter is explicitly the half-angle, and the removable singularities are filled in.
fate: This is the rank-one compact character formula, used as the test case for \citet[compact case]{kirillov1968characters}. It was known before the lecture, although its orbit interpretation is the point of the new presentation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Ordinary universal principal bundles and characteristic classes
notes: \(E_G\to B_G\) is called universal; \(\pi_k(E_G)=0\) for \(k>0\). Characteristic classes are \(H^q(B_G;A)\), and more generally \(h(B_G)\) for a contravariant homotopy functor.
statement: For numerable principal bundles over paracompact Hausdorff bases, a contractible free universal \(G\)-space classifies bundles by homotopy classes \([X,BG]\). A class \(a\in H^q(BG;A)\) gives \(c_a(P)=f_P^*a\). The analogous statement for a contravariant homotopy functor uses the universal pullback class and its naturality. Vanishing higher homotopy groups alone must be supplemented by connectedness and suitable CW-type hypotheses to infer contractibility.
reconstruction: Numerability, paracompactness, and the distinction between weak and actual contractibility are supplied.
fate: This is the conventional background contrasted with the new category in \citet[Introduction]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. The notebook uses aspherical for weak contractibility, rather than the modern condition of vanishing \(\pi_k\) only for \(k>1\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Loss of noncompact information under homotopy equivalence
notes: A maximal compact subgroup is said to be homotopy equivalent to the group, and their classifying spaces homotopy equivalent.
statement: If \(G\) is a Lie group with finitely many connected components and \(K\) a maximal compact subgroup, \(G/K\) is contractible and \(BK\to BG\) is a homotopy equivalence in the usual classifying-space theory. This assertion is not a theorem for an arbitrary topological group merely possessing some compact subgroup.
reconstruction: The Lie-group and finite-component hypotheses are restored.
fate: \citet[Introduction]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} explicitly starts from this loss of information and motivates the new characteristic theory.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: A classifying theory retaining the noncompact group
notes: Gelfand asks for the actual classifying space of a noncompact group, without identifying it with its maximal compact subgroup; bases should be Hausdorff, with a new local-triviality requirement agreeing with the usual one on completely regular bases.
statement: For a closed linear Lie group \(G\), construct a category of principal \(G\)-bundles over Hausdorff spaces, together with sufficiently large universal objects, such that ordinary locally trivial bundles over completely regular bases are included and natural characteristic operations retain information about \(G\), not merely the homotopy type of \(BG\).
reconstruction: The informal request is made precise by the definitions and theorems in the three consecutive Fuchs talks.
fate: \citet[\S\S1--2 and 4]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} supplies the intended category, universal frame spaces, cohomological calculation, and classification of natural operations. The scope is a specified category and an arbitrarily large index set; it is not one ordinary CW space classifying all such bases.
present_status: As of November 2026, this precise linear-group programme is answered by the 1967 paper, with a more general elementary-object formulation in 1968. The broad phrase actual classifying space alone does not define an additional open problem.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: The rejected cone test and Kazhdan's obstruction
notes: For each \(x\), an equivariant map \(E\to CG\) is required to identify the fiber with the cone base. Kazhdan notes that cone height descends to a continuous real function on \(X\); the definition is rejected.
statement: An equivariant map to \(CG\), nonzero on a selected fiber, yields a scalar height function on the base and a local equivariant chart on its nonzero set. Over a completely regular base a local chart can be multiplied by a continuous cutoff to produce such a map. Requiring this construction over arbitrary Hausdorff bases introduces scalar separation unavailable on the ray quotient considered next.
reconstruction: The obstruction explains why the criterion fails for the intended enlarged category. It does not assert that the cone criterion is logically inconsistent or fails for ordinary numerable bundles.
fate: The successful frame-space replacement is given by \citet[\S1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}; the exact cone objection is recorded in the seminar rather than promoted there to a separately numbered theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.
speaker: D. A. Kazhdan

title: Global fiberwise linear charts over Hausdorff bases
notes: For \(G\subset GL(n,\mathbb R)\), form \(E^\#=E\times_G\mathbb R^n\). For every prescribed base point there must be a continuous map \(E^\#\to\mathbb R^n\), linear on all fibers and invertible on the selected fiber.
statement: Use the quotient topology on the associated vector bundle and require global continuous fiberwise linear maps that are isomorphisms on each individually chosen fiber. No support restriction is imposed. This condition implies the usual local trivialization around that fiber; it agrees with ordinary local triviality over completely regular bases. Over merely Hausdorff bases it is an additional specified condition, not a consequence of local triviality alone.
reconstruction: The quantifier for every chosen fiber and the distinction from arbitrary ordinary Hausdorff bundles are made explicit.
fate: This is the principal-bundle category of \citet[\S1, definition preceding Proposition 1.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. Its deliberate use of global linear maps replaces the unsuccessful scalar cutoff construction.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Recovering the principal bundle requires its reduction
notes: The first line says that \(E\) is recovered from \(E^\#\).
statement: The full frame bundle of a rank-\(n\) vector bundle recovers a principal \(GL(n,\mathbb R)\)-bundle. For a proper closed subgroup \(G\), recovering the original principal \(G\)-bundle requires retaining its \(G\)-reduction inside that frame bundle. The underlying associated vector bundle alone generally forgets that reduction.
reconstruction: The missing reduction is an elementary categorical correction, not a claim that the published construction fails.
fate: The frame construction in \citet[\S1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} retains the group action. It does not justify an inverse from bare vector bundles for every subgroup \(G\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The Hausdorff ray quotient with no nonconstant scalar functions
notes: For the additive group \(\mathbb R\) acting by positive homotheties, the total space is written \(\mathbb R^\infty\); the quotient \(S\) is Hausdorff but every continuous real function on it is constant. A cylinder-neighborhood argument is sketched.
statement: Let \(E=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\setminus\{0\}\) have the product topology and let \(t\in\mathbb R\) act by \(x\mapsto e^t x\). The quotient of positive rays is Hausdorff and every continuous map \(S=E/\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is constant. The quotient bundle meets the specified global linear-chart condition. It has no continuous section: the coordinates of such a section would all be constant, making its image a single point.
reconstruction: The zero vector is removed and the additive-to-multiplicative identification is specified.
fate: The example and the cylinder proof occur in \citet[Introduction, pp.33--35 in the Russian original]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. Deleting zero is indispensable to the free action and is explicit in the publication.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The proposed weighted cross-section is not a section of all rays
notes: The notebook suggests examining the purported section \(\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}|x_n|/(1+|x_n|)=1/2\), to see that the resulting map is discontinuous.
statement: This level set does not meet every nonzero positive ray. On a ray supported only at coordinate \(m\ge2\), the left side is always less than \(2^{-m}\le1/4\); for a ray supported only at coordinate 1 it tends to \(1/2\) but never reaches it. Consequently it cannot first define a global set-theoretic selector whose continuity is then tested.
reconstruction: The one-coordinate test is an editorial check. The literal denominator \(1+|x_n|\) and level \(1/2\) were checked against the scan.
fate: The no-section theorem is independently proved in \citet[Introduction]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}; the specific displayed selector is not needed. The failure is an immediate calculation from the handwritten formula.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Universal targets indexed by sufficiently large products
notes: Every bundle maps to the ray-bundle model built from a product of copies of \(\mathbb R\) of sufficiently large cardinality; the map need not be unique.
statement: In the specified category, collecting enough global fiberwise linear charts yields an equivariant map into a frame-space universal bundle indexed by a set \(I\) depending on the given bundle. In rank one this gives the positive-ray construction. Universality means existence of such a bundle morphism and pullback representation; it is not uniqueness of an actual map.
fate: \citet[Proposition 1.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} proves the construction. The variable cardinality is a substantive part of the statement, developed explicitly at the next lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Two-denominator Feynman parametrization
notes: \(1/(ab)=\int_0^1(at+b(1-t))^{-2}\,dt\), described as a good formula of Feynman and a partial-fraction decomposition.
statement: For positive real \(a,b\), \[\frac1{ab}=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{(ta+(1-t)b)^2}.\] The same equality holds for nonzero complex \(a,b\) when the segment \(ta+(1-t)b\) avoids zero. At \(a=b\) the integrand is constant; otherwise integrate its elementary antiderivative.
reconstruction: The denominator-nonvanishing hypothesis and equal-parameter case are supplied.
fate: This is the exponent-one instance of the beta-integral denominator identity; see \citet[\S5.12, Euler beta integral]{nist2026beta}. The seminar attribution names Feynman's useful parametrization, not a new result proved in 1967.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Three denominators and the missing factorial
statement: With ordinary coordinate measure \(dt_1dt_2\) on \(\Delta=\{t_1,t_2\ge0:t_1+t_2\le1\}\), and \(a,b,c>0\), the correct identity is \[\frac1{abc}=2\int_\Delta\frac{dt_1dt_2}{(at_1+bt_2+c(1-t_1-t_2))^3}.\] More generally the \(m\)-denominator numerator factor is \((m-1)!\) for unit powers.
reconstruction: The notebook explicitly uses \(dt_1dt_2\), so normalized probability measure on the simplex is not silently substituted.
fate: The factor follows from the beta-integral normalization \citep[\S5.12]{nist2026beta}. Taking \(a=b=c=1\) already detects the error: the written right side equals the triangle's area \(1/2\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Commuting continuous interval maps need not share a fixed point
notes: The common-fixed-point hypothesis for two commuting continuous maps of an interval has a counterexample.
statement: There exist continuous maps \(f,g:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) with \(f\circ g=g\circ f\) but \(\operatorname{Fix}(f)\cap\operatorname{Fix}(g)=\varnothing\). Thus the fixed-point property of an interval for individual maps does not extend to arbitrary commuting pairs.
fate: \citet[main construction, pp.77--92]{boyce1969commuting} gives a counterexample. His paper was received 9 January 1967, revised 1 December 1967, and published in 1969; it cites Huneke's independent 1967 announcement. The notebook therefore records circulating results, not a problem still unresolved at the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the continuous common-fixed-point conjecture is false. The 1969 publication date must not conceal the 1967 circulation documented in the primary paper.

title: A fixed point of one map that is periodic for the other
notes: If the commuting maps are differentiable, there is a point fixed for one and \ru{конечной кратности} for the other; the English translation says of finite multiplicity.
statement: A precise established version is: if \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is continuously differentiable and \(g:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) is continuous with \(fg=gf\), then for some \(x\) and integer \(n\ge1\), \(f(x)=x\) and \(g^n(x)=x\). The Russian phrase here concerns finite period under iteration, not multiplicity of a zero.
reconstruction: The statement uses the verified \(C^1\) formulation and identifies finite multiplicity as finite period; it does not infer a common fixed point.
fate: The identifiable result is \citet[pp.353--355]{schwartz1965periodic}. The publisher metadata, the reference in \citet[references]{boyce1969commuting}, and the explicit statement in \citet[Introduction, pp.269--270]{alikhanikoopaei1998commuting} were checked; the Schwartz proof itself was not available in readable full text in this audit. Accordingly the exact weakening from \(C^1\) to merely differentiable maps is not asserted.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The bundle category and its characteristic operations
notes: The free action, the global fiberwise linear-chart condition, and equivariant bundle morphisms are restated. \(h_{\mathrm{alg}}(G)\) denotes all characteristic classes formed from a contravariant functor \(h\).
statement: Fix a closed subgroup \(G\subset GL(n,\mathbb R)\). Objects are the principal bundles over Hausdorff bases satisfying the global chart condition of 1967-132.5; morphisms are equivariant maps covering continuous base maps. A characteristic operation assigns \(c(\xi)\in h(X)\) to each object naturally under pullback. No vanishing of the chart map outside a prescribed neighborhood is required.
fate: \citet[\S1 and the beginning of \S2]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} formalizes this category and its natural operations.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Cohomology with the sheaf of continuous real functions
notes: The coefficient sheaf called \(\mathbb R\) consists of germs of continuous real functions. The notes say \(H^q(X,\mathbb R)=0\) for paracompact \(X\).
statement: Write \(\mathcal C_X\) for the sheaf of continuous real functions. On a paracompact Hausdorff space it is fine, so \(H^q(X;\mathcal C_X)=0\) for \(q>0\). Degree zero is \(C(X,\mathbb R)\), usually nonzero. The characteristic groups \(H^q_{\mathrm{alg}}(G;\mathbb R)\) classify natural classes with values in this sheaf cohomology over the enlarged category, not ordinary singular-cohomology characteristic classes.
reconstruction: The notation \(\mathcal C_X\) separates the variable-function sheaf from the constant real sheaf used in the compact-dual calculation.
fate: The notation and vanishing are the setup of \citet[\S2]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. Positive degree is implicit in the seminar parenthesis and is restored here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Compact-dual calculation in the semisimple case
notes: For semisimple \(G\) with finitely many components, \(H^q_{\mathrm{alg}}(G)=H^q(\bar G/K;\mathbb R)\), with constant coefficients on the right; \(K\) is maximal compact and \(\bar G\) a compact form.
statement: For connected semisimple linear \(G\), let \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p\) be its Cartan decomposition, and choose the compact dual pair with Lie algebras \(\mathfrak g_u=\mathfrak k\oplus i\mathfrak p\) and \(\mathfrak k\). Then \(H^*_{\mathrm{alg}}(G;\mathbb R)\cong H^*(G_u/K_u;\mathbb R)\), with the compatible global compact dual and component actions included when \(G\) is disconnected.
reconstruction: The Lie-algebra construction avoids an unjustified assertion that every chosen maximal compact subgroup embeds unchanged in an arbitrarily chosen compact global form.
fate: This is \citet[Theorem 2.9]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. It concerns real cohomology and the compact symmetric dual, not replacement of the original ordinary classifying space \(BG\) by \(G_u/K_u\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The linear-group example and the sphere ambiguity
notes: For \(GL(n,\mathbb R)\), the notes name \(U(n)\) and \(O(n)\), then write: second order, as for \(S^2\).
statement: The reductive compact dual for \(GL(n,\mathbb R)/O(n)\) is \(U(n)/O(n)\). The rank-two semisimple example with spherical dual is instead \(SL(2,\mathbb R)/SO(2)\), whose compact dual is \(SU(2)/SO(2)\simeq S^2\). These spaces cannot be conflated: \(\dim U(2)/O(2)=3\), whereas \(\dim S^2=2\).
reconstruction: The missing transition from the reductive \(GL(n)\) example to \(SL(2)\) is flagged, not silently supplied as notebook wording.
fate: \citet[Theorem 2.9 and its examples]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} supports the semisimple example. The scan does not insert \(SL(2)\) before the sphere remark, so the intended change of group is an emendation, not a resolved transcription.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Invariant forms compute the characteristic cohomology
notes: For a nonsemisimple group one takes \(G/K\), its \(G\)-invariant differential forms, and the cohomology of their differential complex.
statement: For a closed linear Lie group in the category under discussion, \[H^q_{\mathrm{alg}}(G;\mathbb R)\cong H^q\bigl(\Omega^*(G/K)^G,d\bigr).\] Exterior differentiation preserves invariance. This is invariant-form, or relative Lie-algebra, cohomology; it need not equal the de Rham cohomology of the contractible space \(G/K\).
fate: The exact result is \citet[Theorem 2.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. The qualification about invariant forms explains how a nonzero answer survives when the underlying homogeneous space is contractible.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Compact groups and the additive real group
notes: For compact groups everything is trivial. For \(\mathbb R\), the answer is \(\mathbb R\) in degrees 0 and 1 and zero above, with representatives \(1\) and \(dx\).
statement: If \(G\) is compact, the invariant-form complex on \(G/G\) has \(H^0=\mathbb R\) and \(H^q=0\) for \(q>0\). For \(G=(\mathbb R,+)\), the complex of translation-invariant forms is \(\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\,dx\to0\) with zero differential, giving exactly the stated groups.
reconstruction: The degree-zero exception and the zero differential are supplied explicitly.
fate: These are direct instances of \citet[Theorem 2.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. The word trivial refers to positive degrees, not degree zero.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Natural principal H-bundles are induced by homomorphisms
notes: \(EH_{\mathrm{alg}}(G)=\operatorname{Hom}(G,H)\), more precisely continuous homomorphisms modulo conjugacy in \(H\).
statement: For the specified category of principal \(G\)-bundles and a topological group \(H\), natural assignments of isomorphism classes of ordinary locally trivial principal \(H\)-bundles correspond to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,H)/H\). A homomorphism \(\phi\) acts by extension of structure group \(E\mapsto E\times_\phi H\); conjugate homomorphisms give naturally isomorphic assignments.
fate: This is \citet[Theorem 4.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}. The paper allows ordinary local triviality for \(H\)-bundles; when \(H\) is a Lie group, using the enlarged condition gives the same answer.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Frames in a product and universal bundle morphisms
notes: \(\mathcal E_G^I\) consists of \(n\)-frames in \(\mathbb R^I\) with the Tychonoff topology. \(GL(n,\mathbb R)\) and \(G\) act, and \(S_G^I=\mathcal E_G^I/G\); every bundle maps into one for sufficiently large \(I\).
statement: Let \(F_n(\mathbb R^I)\) be ordered linearly independent \(n\)-tuples, equivalently injective linear maps \(\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^I\), with the subspace topology inherited from \((\mathbb R^I)^n\). Precomposition gives a free action of \(G\subset GL(n,\mathbb R)\). Taking sufficiently many global charts gives a bundle morphism into \(F_n(\mathbb R^I)\to F_n(\mathbb R^I)/G\). The total space depends on \(n,I\), while the quotient and action depend on \(G\).
fate: \citet[\S1, Proposition 1.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} proves this exact universal construction.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: A countable-coordinate lemma for frame spaces
notes: For every continuous real function on \(\mathcal E_G^I\), there is \(J\subset I\) with \(I\setminus J\) at most countable such that its restriction to \(\mathcal E_G^J\) is constant.
statement: Embed \(F_n(\mathbb R^J)\) into \(F_n(\mathbb R^I)\) by setting coordinates outside \(J\) equal to zero. Every continuous real-valued function on the latter has a constant restriction to such a subspace for some co-countable \(J\). The statement does not guarantee a nonempty subspace when \(I\) is itself countable and too many coordinates have been removed.
reconstruction: The zero-extension inclusion and the possibly vacuous small-index case are stated explicitly.
fate: The exact lemma is \citet[Proposition 1.3]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}; it is one of the technical reasons large product-indexed universal spaces behave differently from familiar CW models.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: A pointed G-space with an admissible semigroup
notes: \(S\subset\operatorname{Map}(T,T)\) has the compact-open topology, contains the \(G\)-action, and is stable under left and right multiplication by it. The axioms specify a fixed point, an \(S\)-contraction, faithfulness, closedness of \(G\), and nearby maps that are embeddings.
statement: The published elementary \(G\)-object consists of a pointed space \(T\), a topological semigroup \(A\) acting faithfully and fixing the point, an embedded subgroup \(G\), and a contraction through \(A\). Crucially, a neighborhood \(W\supset G\) consists of invertible elements and admits a right-equivariant retraction \(\lambda:W\to G\), with \(\lambda(ag)=\lambda(a)g\) and \(\lambda(g)=g\). This last condition is stronger than merely saying nearby maps are topological embeddings.
reconstruction: The published definition is stated separately from the recorded six-axiom list. No equivalence of the two axiom systems is claimed.
fate: \citet[\S1, axioms 1--4]{gelfandfuchs1968classifying} is the subsequent formulation, received 17 April 1968 and published that year. Its stronger axiom is necessary to identify what was actually proved.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Linear and cone elementary objects
notes: The examples are \(T=\mathbb R^n\), with all linear maps, and \(T=CG\), with the group action and contractions to the apex. The latter is described as a product of cones with the all-apex point removed.
statement: For a closed linear Lie subgroup \(G\), take \(T=\mathbb R^n\) and \(A=\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^n)\). For a topological group, take the cone of pairs \((g,t)\), \(t\ge0\), with all \((g,0)\) identified, and multiplication \((g,t)(h,s)=(gh,ts)\). The cone example has invertible nonapex elements. The positive-ray example uses multiplication by \(e^u\), with the zero sequence deleted.
fate: These are \citet[\S1, Examples 1--2]{gelfandfuchs1968classifying}. The last deleted point is essential to freeness, as in the September ray construction.

title: Universal embeddings versus the published coordinate-invertible model
notes: The universal total space is said to be every embedding \(T\to T^I\) whose coordinate maps lie in \(S\). In the linear example this is the frame space.
statement: The 1968 construction instead takes tuples \((a_i)\in A^I\) with at least one coordinate invertible in \(A\), equipped with the diagonal right \(G\)-action. Such a tuple gives an embedding \(T\to T^I\), but the converse need not hold: a linear injection into a product can be assembled from singular coordinate maps. Thus the earlier all-frame model and the later coordinate-invertible model must not be identified pointwise.
reconstruction: The distinction is explicit: the 1968 universal object is a related construction, not verbatim the set of all embeddings in the notebook.
fate: \citet[\S2, Propositions 3--4 and Theorem 1]{gelfandfuchs1968classifying} proves universality for this published model. The all-frame linear model had already been treated in \citet[Proposition 1.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Finite products are finite approximations, not universal EG
notes: For finite \(I\), the notes call the linear case the usual classifying space and the cone case Milnor's construction with a minor modification.
statement: Finite-dimensional Stiefel and Grassmann spaces classify bundles only subject to dimension or embedding restrictions; their total spaces are not generally contractible universal \(EG\) spaces. Likewise, a finite cone-product or finite join is an approximation. Universal models require an appropriate infinite construction and its stated topology, or the sufficiently large index set tailored to the bundle.
reconstruction: The sentence is interpreted as referring to familiar finite stages, rather than silently changing finite to infinite in the transcription.
fate: The large-index quantifier in \citet[Proposition 1.1]{gelfandfuchs1967topology} and \citet[\S2]{gelfandfuchs1968classifying} supplies the precise interpretation. The literal finite-index universal claim is too strong.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Local T-triviality and universal pullback representation
notes: For each \(x\), the associated \(T\)-bundle has a global map to \(T\), an allowed map on every fiber and a homeomorphism at \(x\). Every bundle over a Hausdorff base maps to the universal one.
statement: Under the published elementary-object axioms, require that for every \(x\) there is a continuous associated-bundle map to \(T\) whose restriction, written in any principal frame, belongs to \(A\), and is invertible in \(A\) on the selected fiber. Such bundles are ordinarily locally trivial; ordinary locally trivial bundles over completely regular bases satisfy this condition. Collecting these maps gives the universal morphism for sufficiently large \(I\).
reconstruction: The stronger semigroup assumptions and invertibility requirement are retained from the publication.
fate: \citet[Propositions 1--2 and Theorem 1]{gelfandfuchs1968classifying} proves these statements. Mere homeomorphism as a map of \(T\), without invertibility in the specified semigroup, is not the complete published hypothesis.

title: Independence of the elementary object
notes: \(H^q_{\mathrm{alg}}(G;\mathbb R)\) does not depend on \(T,S\); the notes add that a group \(A\) may replace \(\mathbb R\).
statement: For a paracompact topological group \(G\) and elementary \(G\)-objects satisfying the published axioms, the characteristic groups with coefficients in a fixed topological \(G\)-module are independent of the chosen object. The coefficient sheaf is the sheaf of continuous sections of the associated module bundle. One must hold the coefficient sheaf and the naturality category fixed; the notebook does not specify which arbitrary coefficient groups or sheaves its parenthetical extension includes.
reconstruction: The real-coefficient construction is the definite statement; the unrestricted coefficient parenthesis is not upgraded into an unproved generalization.

title: Analytic linearization of a semisimple action at a fixed point
notes: The planned Kushnirenko talk is summarized as: an analytic action of a semisimple group near a fixed point is linear.
statement: Let a finite-dimensional real semisimple Lie algebra act by germs of real-analytic vector fields vanishing at a point of a real-analytic manifold. There are local real-analytic coordinates in which the action is its linear isotropy representation. Equivalently, an analytic local action of the corresponding connected group is locally analytically linearizable at the fixed point.
reconstruction: The local germ formulation and connected-group qualification state the precise theorem behind the one-line announcement.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1]{kushnirenko1967linearization} proves the result; the note was received 16 November 1966 and published in the first 1967 issue, before this programme. The smooth category cannot simply replace the analytic one.

title: Programme labels that do not specify mathematical assertions
notes: The programme mentions conditions for invariant measures, a solution of Selberg's problem, Pham's work, \(P^\lambda\), Grassmann analysis, and several names without a theorem statement.
statement: These entries identify proposed topics and speakers only. In particular, neither the invariant-measure conditions nor which Selberg problem is meant is stated here. No mathematical quantifiers can be recovered solely from these programme labels.
fate: The adjacent later records, and the earlier Kazhdan material in 1966-101, provide context but do not turn this plan into a uniquely stated new theorem. No exact publication match is assigned to the topic list.

title: Interpolation pairs of compatible Banach couples
notes: All four endpoint Banach spaces are embedded in a common topological linear space on each side; every endpoint-bounded linear operator must map the intermediate pair boundedly.
statement: Let \((E_0,E_1)\) and \((F_0,F_1)\) be compatible Banach couples. Intermediate spaces satisfy \(E_0\cap E_1\hookrightarrow E\hookrightarrow E_0+E_1\) and similarly for \(F\). The pair \((E,F)\) is an interpolation pair if each linear \(A:E_0+E_1\to F_0+F_1\), bounded from \(E_i\) to \(F_i\) for \(i=0,1\), restricts boundedly from \(E\) to \(F\). Exactness is the stronger assertion that the intermediate operator norm is at most the maximum endpoint norm.
reconstruction: The common-domain sum space and the distinction between boundedness and exactness are supplied.
fate: This is the standard operator-interpolation framework used by \citet[opening definitions]{mityagin1965interpolation} and \citet[\S2]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact}. The lecture later asks an exact-norm question, which must be distinguished from bounded interpolation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Symmetric function spaces and basic inclusions
notes: A Banach space of summable functions on \([0,1]\) is symmetric if it has the ideal property and its norm is invariant under measure-preserving transformations; then \(L_\infty\subset E\subset L_1\).
statement: On the Lebesgue probability interval, a rearrangement-invariant Banach function space has the ideal property \(|f|\le|g|\Rightarrow\|f\|_E\le\|g\|_E\), and equimeasurable absolute values have equal norms. In the usual Banach-function-space setting, \(L^\infty\hookrightarrow E\hookrightarrow L^1\) continuously. A Fatou property, order continuity, or full symmetry is an additional property and must not be hidden inside the two displayed axioms.
reconstruction: Equimeasurability and continuous inclusions are the modern formulation; the extra regularity assumptions are explicitly kept separate.
fate: The distinction matters in \citet[Theorems 1 and 3]{mityagin1965interpolation} and in \citet[\S1]{boyd1969indices}. It is precisely why the unqualified interpolation claims later in the notes require care.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Lorentz, associate Marcinkiewicz, and Orlicz examples
notes: The examples are \(\int_0^1f^*\,d\psi\) for monotone \(\psi\). The displayed dual norm is \[\sup_e\int_e|f|/\psi(m(e)).\] Orlicz spaces, including \(L^p\), are also listed.
statement: For an increasing concave function \(\psi\) with \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\psi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), the Lorentz norm is \(\|f\|_{\Lambda_\psi}=\int_0^1f^*(t)\,d\psi(t)\). Its associate norm is \(\sup_{0<t\le1}\psi(t)^{-1}\int_0^t f^*(s)\,ds\), equivalently the supremum over measurable sets of measure \(t\). For a Young function \(\Phi\), the Luxemburg Orlicz norm is \(\inf\{c>0:\int\Phi(|f|/c)\le1\}\); \(\Phi(u)=u^p\) gives \(L^p\).
reconstruction: Concavity, positivity, the endpoint normalization, and the meaning of dual as associate norm are supplied.
fate: Lorentz and associate spaces are used explicitly in \citet[\S1]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact} and \citet[\S1]{boyd1969indices}. Monotonicity alone is insufficient to guarantee that the displayed Lorentz functional is a Banach norm.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Riesz--Thorin interpolation
notes: The first step is named as the Riesz--Thorin theorem.
statement: For a linear operator bounded \(L^{p_i}(\mu)\to L^{q_i}(\nu)\) with norms \(M_i\), \(1\le p_i,q_i\le\infty\), the standard complex interpolation theorem gives \(L^{p_\theta}\to L^{q_\theta}\) with norm at most \(M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\), where \(p_\theta^{-1}=(1-\theta)p_0^{-1}+\theta p_1^{-1}\) and similarly for \(q_\theta\). The operator must be consistently defined on the endpoint sum.
reconstruction: The full familiar statement fills in the named theorem; endpoint measurability conventions are the standard sigma-finite setting.
fate: The theorem is background for the improvement discussed in \citet[Introduction]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact}. The notebook gives no separate proof or novelty claim.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Weak endpoint bounds and Marcinkiewicz interpolation
notes: The distribution-function bound is \(n_{Af}(\tau)^{1/q_i}\le C\|f\|_{p_i}/\tau\), described as weaker endpoint information.
statement: This means \(\|Af\|_{L^{q_i,\infty}}\le C_i\|f\|_{L^{p_i}}\). For example, if \(1\le p_0<p_1<\infty\) and a sublinear operator has weak types \((p_0,p_0)\) and \((p_1,p_1)\), it is strongly bounded on \(L^p\) for \(p_0<p<p_1\). More general off-diagonal versions require their own exponent hypotheses; the two endpoint inequalities alone are not a statement about every possible intermediate exponent.
reconstruction: A safe diagonal theorem and the precise weak-space interpretation are separated from the later improving theorem.
fate: \citet[Introduction and \S2]{boyd1969indices} uses this precise weak-type framework, and \citet[Theorem 2]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact} gives the off-diagonal Lorentz version relevant here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The Dikarev--Matsaev Lorentz improvement and optimality
notes: For improving operators \(q_i>p_i\), the intermediate image lies in a Lorentz space narrower than \(L^q\), and this image space is minimal for all operators with the endpoint bounds.
statement: Take \(1<p_0<p_1<\infty\), distinct \(1<q_0,q_1<\infty\), and \(0<\theta<1\). Interpolation of weak endpoint maps gives \(L^{p,p}\to L^{q,p}\), where the reciprocal exponents are interpolated linearly. Since \(L^{p,p}=L^p\) and \(L^{q,p}\subset L^q\) when \(p<q\), this improves the target. The published sharpness theorem quantifies over all endpoint-admissible operators on nonatomic measure spaces, with an infinite source measure in its stated general form.
reconstruction: The Lorentz second index \(p\) and the measure-space restriction in the sharpness theorem are supplied; minimality is not asserted for every one fixed operator.
fate: \citet[Theorems 2--3]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact}, received 25 September 1965 and published in 1966, gives both the target and the quantified optimality. This is earlier work being reported by Krein.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Mityagin exact interpolation and symmetric norms
notes: Every contraction on \(L^1\) and \(L^\infty\) is a contraction on exactly the symmetric spaces; a two-dimensional square-and-diamond diagram motivates the statement.
statement: In finite dimensions, operators contractive for both \(\ell^1\) and \(\ell^\infty\) contract every symmetric norm; signed coordinate permutations and their convex hull give the elementary model. In function spaces, Mityagin proves the corresponding exact interpolation theorem for minimal symmetric ideals, and separately for maximal ideals. A fully symmetric Banach function space is an exact interpolation space for \((L^1,L^\infty)\). The two symmetry axioms alone, without the relevant regularity or majorization property, must not be substituted for these hypotheses.
reconstruction: The finite-dimensional illustration and the infinite-dimensional theorem are distinguished. Full symmetry means monotonicity under Hardy--Littlewood submajorization.
fate: \citet[Theorems 1--3]{mityagin1965interpolation} is the exact named source, received 3 December 1963 and published in 1965. Its minimal/maximal qualifications are absent from the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Fundamental function and dyadic ratios
notes: \(\|\chi_e\|_E=\varphi(m(e))\); \(\ell_E=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\varphi(2t)/\varphi(t)\), \(u_E=\limsup\), with \(1\le\ell_E\le u_E\le2\), and both equal \(2^{1/p}\) for \(L^p\).
statement: For a rearrangement-invariant space on \([0,1]\), the fundamental function is \(\varphi_E(t)=\|\chi_{[0,t]}\|_E\). Monotonicity and the triangle inequality give \(1\le\varphi_E(2t)/\varphi_E(t)\le2\) when \(0<t\le1/2\). For \(L^p\), \(\varphi(t)=t^{1/p}\), with the standard interpretation for \(p=\infty\). These ratios measure only indicator functions, not the norm of the dilation operator on all of \(E\).
fate: These are the invariants used in \citet[Theorem 1]{semenov1965interpolation}. Their distinction from dilation indices is made explicit in \citet[\S3]{sharpley1975interpolation}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The fundamental-function criterion fails in full generality
notes: Semenov's first theorem is recorded as: every operator bounded on all \(L^p\), \(1<p<\infty\), is bounded on \(E\) if and only if \(1<\ell_E\le u_E<2\).
statement: The stated criterion is false for arbitrary symmetric spaces, even with separability added. The norm of every dilation, rather than only its values on indicators, controls the general interpolation property. For a rearrangement-invariant Banach function space with the Fatou property, writing the Boyd exponents in the convention \(0\le\beta_E\le\alpha_E\le1\), the correct nonendpoint condition is \(0<\beta_E\le\alpha_E<1\). More generally all weak-type \((p,p),(q,q)\) operators act on \(E\) exactly when \(1/q<\beta_E\le\alpha_E<1/p\).
reconstruction: The modern Boyd-index theorem is a corrected replacement, not an assertion that Semenov used those indices. The all-\(L^p\) consequence follows by choosing finite endpoints around the Boyd exponents; the Hardy operators also show necessity.
fate: The historical claim is \citet[Theorem 1]{semenov1965interpolation}; the later general argument appears in \citet{semenov1968interpolation}. \citet[\S3, pp.122--125]{sharpley1975interpolation} explicitly disproves the underlying theorem using a space with \(\varphi(t)=\sqrt t\) but an endpoint Boyd exponent. The replacement is \citet[Theorem 1]{boyd1969indices}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the historical general criterion is refuted; its exact appearance in the literature is not evidence of correctness. Fundamental-function criteria remain valid in appropriately restricted classes where they control the dilation norms.

title: The improving symmetric-space criterion and its limitation
notes: For operators \(L^{1/\alpha}\to L^{1/(\alpha-\Delta)}\), \(\alpha_0<\alpha<\alpha_1\), the notes assert \(E\to E_\Delta\) when \(2^{\alpha_0}<\ell_E\le u_E<2^{\alpha_1}\), with \(\|f\|_{E_\Delta}=\|t^{-\Delta}f^*(t)\|_E\).
statement: The displayed target functional specializes, for \(E=L^p\) and \(0<\Delta<1/p\), to \(\bigl(\int_0^1[f^*(t)]^p t^{-p\Delta}dt\bigr)^{1/p}\), the Lorentz \(L^{q,p}\) functional with \(1/q=1/p-\Delta\). This correctly explains the classical improving case. The claimed extension to every symmetric \(E\), controlled only by its fundamental-function ratios, is not a valid general theorem; additional dilation or majorization hypotheses are needed.
reconstruction: The exponent is read as \(1/(\alpha-\Delta)\), consistent with the target functional and improving-operator discussion. The general false claim is separated from its valid \(L^p\) specialization.
fate: \citet[Theorem 3]{semenov1967fourier} and \citet[Theorem 2]{semenov1968interpolation} are the exact historical continuation; the latter manuscript was received 7 June 1967. The inaccuracies and failed underlying representation theorem are documented in \citet[\S3]{sharpley1975interpolation}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the \(L^p\)-to-Lorentz specialization is established, while the unqualified fundamental-function extension is invalid. The printed 1968 theorem is a publication match, not a valid modern resolution.

title: Hausdorff--Young with the conjugate exponent
notes: The written expression is \((|c_k|^p)^{1/p}\le\|f\|_{L^p}\), with no visible summation and with \(p\) on both sides.
statement: On the probability circle, for \(1\le p\le2\) and \(p^{-1}+(p^{\prime})^{-1}=1\), the Fourier coefficients satisfy \(\|\widehat f\|_{\ell^{p^{\prime}}}\le\|f\|_{L^p}\). At \(p=1\) the target is \(\ell^\infty\). A bound on each individual coefficient is much weaker; an \(\ell^p\) bound for general \(p<2\) is not Hausdorff--Young.
reconstruction: The conjugate exponent and summation or supremum are restored. The lack of a summation sign was confirmed in the scan.
fate: This classical endpoint interpolation application is the baseline for \citet[Theorem 4]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact} and the Fourier estimates in \citet[\S2]{semenov1967fourier}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Paley's rearranged-coefficient inequality
notes: The heading is written \ru{Пойя}; the inequality is \((\sum_{k\ge1}k^{p-2}(c_k^*)^p)^{1/p}\le C\|f\|_p\).
statement: For \(1<p\le2\), Fourier coefficients relative to a uniformly bounded orthonormal system satisfy \[\left(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{p-2}(c_k^*)^p\right)^{1/p}\le C_p\|f\|_{L^p},\] where \(c_k^*\) is the decreasing rearrangement of absolute coefficients. This is a Lorentz \(\ell^{p^{\prime},p}\) bound; for the trigonometric system the usual normalization only changes the constant.
reconstruction: The exponent range, orthonormal-system hypotheses, and corrected attribution are supplied.
fate: \citet[Theorem 4]{dikarevmatsaev1966exact} gives the Lorentz estimate. \citet[Theorem 6 and the following paragraph]{semenov1967fourier} explicitly names the \(L^p\) specialization as Paley's theorem, supporting a mathematical-name emendation from the source's Poia/P'olya heading.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Hardy--Littlewood for monotone Fourier coefficients
notes: Monotonically decreasing Fourier coefficients yield two-sided inequalities, attributed to Hardy and Littlewood.
statement: For \(1<p<\infty\) and a nonnegative decreasing sequence \(a_n\to0\), the classical monotone sine-series theorem characterizes \(\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\sin nt\in L^p\) by \(\sum_{n\ge1}n^{p-2}a_n^p<\infty\), with equivalence of the corresponding norms. A parallel cosine-series formulation needs its constant coefficient included. Arbitrary rearrangements of coefficients do not give such a two-sided theorem.
reconstruction: A definite monotone nonnegative sine-series version replaces the unspecified phrase Fourier coefficients.
fate: \citet[Theorem 7 and its specialization paragraph]{semenov1967fourier} explicitly identifies the Hardy--Littlewood result. Its broader symmetric-space extension shares the fundamental-function difficulties discussed above; the classical \(L^p\) assertion is retained separately.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: No Hilbert interpolation space between L1 and L3/2
notes: The notes attribute to Semenov the absence of a Hilbert interpolation space between \(L_1\) and \(L_{1.5}\).
statement: In the nonatomic function-space setting there is no rearrangement-invariant space isomorphic to a Hilbert space with continuous inclusions \(L^{3/2}\hookrightarrow E\hookrightarrow L^1\). Indeed Hilbert type and cotype, applied to disjoint equimeasurable indicators, force \(\varphi_E(1/n)\asymp n^{-1/2}\), while \(L^{3/2}\hookrightarrow E\) forces \(\varphi_E(1/n)\le Cn^{-2/3}\), a contradiction. Consequently no Hilbert interpolation space in this symmetric category exists.
reconstruction: The disjoint-indicator argument is editorial. It uses nonatomicity and Banach-space isomorphism to Hilbert space, not merely equality of norms. The broader abstract-category formulation is not inferred.
fate: The symmetry framework is that of \citet{mityagin1965interpolation}. No exact early Semenov publication for this isolated assertion was identified in the 1965, 1967, and 1968 papers inspected. The elementary argument establishes the qualified claim without assigning it to an unrelated theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Gelfand's request for an abstract description
notes: Gelfand asks for an abstract description of interpolation spaces; the parenthesis says it is unknown whether they are function spaces.
statement: The notes do not specify a Banach couple, the operator category, an isometric versus isomorphic representation, or a required lattice structure. Thus several inequivalent representation and classification questions fit the wording, and no unique quantified conjecture can be extracted.
fate: The inspected Mityagin, Semenov, Boyd, and Sharpley papers address specified function-space interpolation problems. They do not provide an exact match to this unrestricted question. It is retained as an identifiable programme remark, without an invented open-problem identifier.
present_status: As of November 2026, the historical question remains underdetermined by this record. It should not be reported as a single still-open theorem problem.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Hyperbolic toral automorphisms and Lebesgue spectrum
notes: The integer matrix defines a two-torus map. Irrational eigenvalues are said to imply real eigenvalues, ergodicity, and countably multiple Lebesgue spectrum.
statement: Let \(A\in SL(2,\mathbb Z)\) satisfy \(|\operatorname{tr}A|>2\). Its toral automorphism preserves Haar probability and is ergodic. Its Koopman operator on the mean-zero subspace of \(L^2(\mathbb T^2)\) is a countable direct sum of bilateral shifts; the constant functions separately contribute the eigenvalue \(1\). Indeed, the Fourier characters indexed by nonzero lattice points split into infinite \(A^{\mathsf T}\)-orbits. Nonrational eigenvalues alone do not imply real eigenvalues: a finite-order rotation matrix is a counterexample.
reconstruction: The statement uses the intended real hyperbolic case; it does not redefine irrational to mean real without saying so.
fate: This is the hyperbolic toral setting of \citet[\S1]{adlerweiss1967entropy}. The Fourier-orbit argument supplies the precise spectral meaning of the notebook sentence; the hyperbolicity hypothesis and removal of constants are indispensable.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Entropy classifies hyperbolic two-torus automorphisms metrically
notes: When does a measurable \(U\) satisfy \(UT_1=T_2U\)? The entropy is \(\log\lambda\), where \(\lambda>1\), and equal entropy is asserted to imply metric similarity, although integral linear conjugacy can fail.
statement: For hyperbolic automorphisms \(T_A,T_B\) of \(\mathbb T^2\), with Haar probability, there is a measure-preserving invertible conjugacy modulo null sets if and only if their entropies agree. Here \(h(T_A)=\log\rho(A)\). Equality of entropy does not generally imply conjugacy of the matrices in \(GL(2,\mathbb Z)\). Merely requiring a measurable map, without invertibility and preservation of measure, is a different and much weaker question.
reconstruction: Metric similarity is interpreted as isomorphism of probability-preserving transformations modulo zero; \(\lambda\) is the modulus of the expanding eigenvalue.
fate: This is exactly the Main Theorem of \citet[\S1]{adlerweiss1967entropy}, communicated on 24 April 1967 and published in June 1967. It was therefore already known at the October lecture, although the notes present its proof programme.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated two-dimensional classification is settled. This occurrence is not an open entropy-classification problem for arbitrary measure-preserving systems.

title: Topological conjugacies are affine under ergodicity
notes: The notes say that if \(U\) is a homeomorphism then it is linear, adding in parentheses that this holds for any compact abelian groups.
statement: If \(A,B\in GL(n,\mathbb Z)\), \(T_A\) is ergodic, and a homeomorphism \(U\) satisfies \(UT_A=T_BU\), then \(U(x)=Cx+c\), with \(C\in GL(n,\mathbb Z)\), \(CA=BC\), and \(T_Bc=c\). Thus \(U\) is linear after imposing \(U(0)=0\). Without ergodicity even the identity transformation admits many nonlinear conjugacies. The unrestricted compact-abelian parenthesis lacks its necessary hypotheses.
reconstruction: The verified theorem is restricted to tori and states the translation term explicitly; the general compact-group extension is not asserted.
fate: \citet[Theorem, pp.1223--1225]{adlerpalais1965homeomorphic} proves precisely the toral affine-rigidity assertion. The paper was received in November 1964 and published in 1965. Its proof does not justify deleting the translation term.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: A primitive two-sided shift of finite type
notes: \(\Omega_\Pi\) consists of bi-infinite sequences \((i_n)\) with \(\pi_{i_ni_{n+1}}=1\), for a finite zero-one matrix. A power of \(\Pi\) is assumed strictly positive.
statement: For a finite zero-one matrix \(A\), let \(\Sigma_A=\{x\in\{1,\ldots,s\}^{\mathbb Z}:A_{x_nx_{n+1}}=1\}\), with the product topology and the coordinate shift \(\sigma\). Primitivity means \(A^k>0\) for some \(k\); it implies topological mixing of this shift. The Borel sigma algebra is generated by finite-coordinate cylinders.
fate: \citet[\S\S2--3]{adlerweiss1967entropy} and \citet[\S\S2--4]{parry1964intrinsic} use this exact finite-state setup. The cylinder sigma algebra mentioned later in the notebook is part of this definition.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The identity, full-shift, and golden-mean examples
notes: The three matrices are \(I_2\), the two-by-two all-ones matrix, and \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The last is left for examination.
statement: For \(I_2\), the shift space consists of two fixed sequences and the matrix is not primitive. The all-ones matrix gives the full two-shift, with entropy \(\log2\). The third matrix forbids consecutive occurrences of symbol \(2\); it is primitive, has Perron eigenvalue \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\), and has entropy \(\log\varphi\).
reconstruction: The forbidden word and entropy of the third matrix are an editorial calculation.
fate: These elementary examples follow directly from the finite-state framework and Perron construction in \citet[Theorems 5 and 7]{parry1964intrinsic}. The last example is worked out here as an annotation to the instruction to examine it.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: The Parry transition probabilities need both Perron vectors
notes: The notebook writes \(\lambda e=\Pi^*e\), then \(p_{ij}=e_j\pi_{ij}/(\lambda e_i)\), and uses \(e_i\) as the stationary weights in the entropy formula.
statement: Let \(A\) be primitive, \(Ar=\lambda r\), \(l^{\mathsf T}A=\lambda l^{\mathsf T}\), with positive vectors normalized by \(l^{\mathsf T}r=1\). Then \(P_{ij}=A_{ij}r_j/(\lambda r_i)\) is stochastic and \(w_i=l_ir_i\) is stationary. The cylinder probability is \(w_{i_0}P_{i_0i_1}\cdots P_{i_{m-1}i_m}\). A left Perron vector cannot replace \(r\) in the displayed row-transition formula for a general nonsymmetric matrix.
reconstruction: The transpose is removed from the right-eigenvector equation, and the separate stationary vector \(w\) replaces the reused letter \(e\).
fate: The correct construction is \citet[Theorem 5]{parry1964intrinsic}, also presented in \citet[\S3]{adlerweiss1967entropy}. Both earlier publications distinguish the two eigenvectors. A nonsymmetric numerical example is recorded in this fragment's computation file.

title: Entropy and uniqueness of the maximal stationary measure
notes: The entropy of a stationary Markov chain is displayed as a weighted sum of row entropies. The preceding chain is said to have entropy \(\log\lambda\) and to be the unique measure of maximal entropy.
statement: For a finite stationary chain with distribution \(w\) and transition matrix \(P\), \(h_\mu(\sigma)=-\sum_iw_i\sum_jP_{ij}\log P_{ij}\), with \(0\log0=0\). For the Parry chain above the coboundary terms \(\log r_j-\log r_i\) cancel by stationarity, leaving \(\log\lambda\). An irreducible finite shift of finite type has this unique invariant probability of maximal entropy; primitivity additionally gives mixing.
reconstruction: The correct stationary weights, invariance restriction, and distinction between irreducibility and primitivity are supplied.
fate: \citet[Theorems 7 and 9]{parry1964intrinsic} proves the entropy and uniqueness results. The notebook's maximization must range over shift-invariant probabilities, rather than all measures on the cylinder sigma algebra.

title: Gelfand on second-order minors and one sign change
notes: Gelfand remarks that if all entries and all second-order minors are positive, the first eigenvector is positive and the second has one sign change. He points to the action on the second exterior power.
statement: For a real \(n\times n\) matrix, \(n\ge2\), with all entries and all ordered two-by-two minors strictly positive, the two eigenvalues of largest modulus are simple and satisfy \(\lambda_1>\lambda_2>0\), with \(\lambda_2>|\lambda_j|\) for \(j\ge3\). A first eigenvector is strictly positive; a second has exactly one sign variation after zero coordinates are omitted. Perron's theorem applied to the matrix and its second compound gives the spectral assertion. Positivity of \(v_1\wedge v_2\) makes the ratios \(v_{2i}/v_{1i}\) strictly monotone, and orthogonality to a positive left Perron vector forces their signs to cross.
reconstruction: The statement separates the precise second-order consequence from the stronger full oscillation theorems, and makes the handling of zero coordinates explicit.
fate: This is an elementary second-compound specialization of the oscillation method of \citet[\S\S4--5, pp.460--466]{gantmacherkrein1937matrices}. The exterior-power proof specified in the notebook is recognizable; no assumption of positivity of all higher minors is needed for this two-eigenvector conclusion.

title: The four-block symbolic matrix
notes: The alphabet has groups of sizes \(p,q,r,s\). From either \(a\)-group one may move to \(a^1\) or \(b^1\); from either \(b\)-group to \(a^2\) or \(b^2\). The equation is \(\lambda^2-(p+s)\lambda+ps-qr=0\), with \(ps-qr=1\).
statement: Order the symbols as \(a^1,a^2,b^1,b^2\). Give all rows in the first two groups the allowed columns \(a^1,b^1\), and all rows in the last two groups the allowed columns \(a^2,b^2\). For positive block sizes the resulting matrix is primitive, has rank two, and has characteristic polynomial \(t^{p+q+r+s-2}(t^2-(p+s)t+ps-qr)\). This reduction follows by restricting to vectors constant on the two row types.
reconstruction: Positivity of the four sizes is imposed for the simple primitive case. Zero-sized or sign-modified geometric cases need their separate conventions.
fate: The construction and characteristic polynomial occur exactly in \citet[\S4]{adlerweiss1967entropy}. The Greek/Roman ambiguity in the notebook's transition labels does not affect the four named blocks or their destinations.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Recoding to a full matrix with one forbidden transition
notes: The second model has \(N\) symbols and every transition except \(N\to1\). The two shifts are called isomorphic, and the coding is said to carry one maximal measure to the other.
statement: Let the positive four-block matrix satisfy \(ps-qr=1\), and set \(N=p+s\). With their respective Parry measures, its shift and the shift defined by \(J_N-E_{N1}\) are measurably isomorphic modulo zero. The second matrix has characteristic polynomial \(t^{N-2}(t^2-Nt+1)\), so the Perron roots and entropies agree. The isomorphism is a variable-block measurable coding, not a global topological conjugacy.
reconstruction: The category of isomorphism and the relation \(N=p+s\) are made explicit. Transposing the single forbidden transition merely changes the symbol/reversal convention.
fate: This is precisely the determinant-one theorem in \citet[\S4]{adlerweiss1967entropy}. The paper proves the almost-everywhere invertible block coding and preservation of the maximal measures; equality of the eigenvalues alone would not prove it.

title: The parenthetical extension to all equal-entropy Markov shifts
notes: A parenthesis refers to isomorphism of any two \(\Omega_\Pi\) with equal entropy, without another proof.
statement: For primitive finite matrices, equip each two-sided shift with its Parry probability. These mixing finite-state Markov systems are Bernoulli, and two are measure-theoretically isomorphic exactly when their entropies agree. This is a statement about probability-preserving systems; equality of entropy does not classify shifts of finite type up to topological conjugacy.
reconstruction: The notebook parenthesis is interpreted in its surrounding maximal-measure and primitive-matrix setting.
fate: The general claim is supplied by the later Bernoulli theory: the 1970 Friedman--Ornstein Markov result and Ornstein's equal-entropy isomorphism theorem are explicitly presented together in \citet[\S5, Theorems 4--5 and references 3, 5]{ornstein1975applications}. That primary author exposition was read; the 1970 original proof was not accessible in this audit. Adler--Weiss's June 1967 proof verifies the preceding special family only.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified measurable statement is established. No unrestricted entropy-only topological classification is asserted.

title: Projective relative periods
notes: \(J(t)=\int_{\gamma^q(t)}\omega(t,\xi)\), with \(t\in\mathbb C^n\), \(\xi\in\mathbb C^{\ell+1}\), a cycle relative to \(W(t)\), and a degree-zero homogeneous form vanishing on \(W(t)\). Homogeneity is said to put the form on \(\mathbb P^\ell\).
statement: A differential form on \(\mathbb C^{\ell+1}\setminus\{0\}\) descends to projective space when it is invariant under scalar multiplication and horizontal for the Euler vector field. For a closed relative \(q\)-form \(\omega_t\) with zero pullback to \(W_t\), integrate over a relative real \(q\)-cycle with boundary in \(W_t\), avoiding the polar locus. The period depends on its relative homology class, and a local family of cycles must be transported continuously away from singular parameters.

title: The degeneracy locus of a moving hyperplane arrangement
notes: \(W(t)=\bigcup_kW_k(t)\) is a union of hyperplanes depending algebraically on \(t\). The set \(S_0[W]\) is where the dimension of an intersection changes.
statement: For a finite algebraic family of projective hyperplanes, the ranks of the matrices defining every subfamily are generically constant. Their rank-drop conditions, given by minors, produce an algebraic discriminant after coefficients and branch choices are placed on the appropriate algebraic parameter space. Outside it the incidence type is locally constant. Singularities involving the polar variety require additional tangency or stratified nontransversality conditions, not only hyperplane intersection ranks.

title: Iterated residues and the cycle on the complete intersection
notes: The notes identify \(\gamma^{q-m}(t)\) with \(\bigcap_jV_j(t)\), write poles \(v_j^{-1-\beta_j}\), and use a quotient of derivatives by powers of \(dv_j\) as a residue notation.
statement: For transverse smooth hypersurfaces \(V_j=\{v_j=0\}\) and a meromorphic \(q\)-form \(\eta\) with simple logarithmic poles, its iterated residue is a \((q-m)\)-form on their complete intersection. A real \((q-m)\)-cycle \(\gamma\) there has an iterated tubular \(q\)-cycle \(\delta^m\gamma\), and, with compatible orientations, \(\int_{\delta^m\gamma}\eta=(2\pi i)^m\int_\gamma\operatorname{Res}_{V_1,\ldots,V_m}\eta\). Higher pole orders are handled by Leray residue classes and pole-order differentiation with the corresponding factorials. Powers of a one-form in the notebook denominator are not ordinary exterior powers.
reconstruction: The simple-pole residue identity states a precise special case. The higher-pole notebook expression is retained as symbolic residue notation, not expanded into an unjustified differential quotient.
fate: The exact higher-pole notation and its reduction to a tubular integral occur in \citet[\S1, formula (3), and \S20, p.352]{leray1967complement}. The published cycle lies on the complete intersection; it is not identical to that algebraic variety.

title: Algebraic singular support of the period
notes: The theorem says that \(J(t)\) has algebraic singular support: it is holomorphic on a covering of the complement of an algebraic set. Leray describes that set in the hyperplane case.
statement: In Leray's projective relative-period setting, assume the integrand has algebraic singular support and impose his non-appui hypothesis for the moving arrangement against the polar and auxiliary algebraic varieties. Then there is an algebraic hypersurface \(S\) in parameter space such that the analytically continued period is holomorphic on the universal covering of its complement. Its singular support lies in the union of the arrangement discriminant and the specified incidence/tangency locus. This permits nontrivial monodromy and transcendental periods.
reconstruction: The omitted non-appui hypothesis is retained by name and its role is explained; the algebraicity assertion concerns the exceptional set, not the value of the integral.
fate: This is \citet[Theorem 1, pp.316--317]{leray1967complement}; its Corollary 1.1 identifies the absolute-cycle case with Nilsson's earlier theorem. The publisher dates \citet{nilsson1964growth} to October 1964, despite later bibliographies sometimes using the volume year 1965. Leray's general relative statement appeared in 1967. Only the absolute-case attribution, not Nilsson's full proof, was independently checked in the latter source.

title: Uniform hyperbolicity and the compact-distance caveat
notes: The \(U\)-condition is illustrated by exponential separation of nearby points in one time direction, followed by contracting and expanding submanifolds of dimensions \(k,\ell\), with \(k+\ell=n\) and uniform transversality.
statement: A \(C^1\) diffeomorphism \(T\) of a compact Riemannian manifold is Anosov if \(TM=E^s\oplus E^u\) is a continuous invariant splitting and there are \(C>0\), \(0<\theta<1\) such that \(\|DT^nv_s\|\le C\theta^n\|v_s\|\) and \(\|DT^{-n}v_u\|\le C\theta^n\|v_u\|\) for all \(n\ge0\). Uniform exponential expansion is a derivative or leafwise local statement. Distances between two fixed distinct points in a compact space cannot grow exponentially for all time.
reconstruction: The derivative definition replaces the globally impossible distance inequality. One may also use intrinsic leaf metrics as in Sinai's publication.
fate: The standard splitting and its stable/unstable interpretation are recalled by \citet[\S1]{sinai1968markov} and, in modern notation, \citet[Definition 2.1]{spatzier2016rigidity}. These were the established Anosov framework by the lecture, not a new consequence of the displayed metric inequality.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Stable manifolds and the choice of contraction constants
notes: Points with exponentially shrinking forward distance form \(\Gamma^{(c)}(x)\); backward shrinking gives \(\Gamma^{(p)}(x)\). The sets are said not to depend on \(a,c\).
statement: For an Anosov diffeomorphism, \(W^s(x)=\{y:d(T^ny,T^nx)\to0\text{ as }n\to+\infty\}\) and the analogous \(W^u(x)\) are immersed leaves tangent to \(E^s,E^u\), of complementary dimensions. Their local plaques vary continuously and are uniformly transverse. For \(C^r\) dynamics the individual leaves have the corresponding smoothness, although transverse regularity is weaker. Changing to admissible weaker exponential estimates does not change the global asymptotic leaf; a fixed local plaque or a prescribed overly fast rate can change the selected set.
reconstruction: Global leaves, local plaques, and the range of admissible exponential rates are distinguished.
fate: \citet[\S1, pp.64--65]{sinai1968markov} explicitly distinguishes leafwise metrics and allowable contraction constants. The notebook's independence of constants is valid only in that standard asymptotic sense.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; the distinctions from the notebook wording remain essential.

title: Linear examples and structural stability
notes: An integral two-by-two matrix of determinant one is given as an example. Smooth periodic nonlinear perturbations remain \(U\)-diffeomorphisms and have the same rotation number; a later sentence attributes topological conjugacy under small perturbations to Anosov.
statement: A toral map \(T_A\), \(A\in GL(n,\mathbb Z)\), is Anosov precisely when no eigenvalue has modulus one. Every sufficiently small \(C^1\) perturbation is Anosov and is topologically conjugate to \(T_A\); more generally every Anosov diffeomorphism is structurally stable in this sense. In dimension two, determinant one alone is insufficient. The stable and unstable asymptotic directions supply the intended rotation/slope information, but there is no single circle rotation number for an arbitrary toral map.
reconstruction: Smallness is in \(C^1\), hyperbolicity is explicit, and the informal rotation-number phrase is not promoted to a new invariant.
fate: The structural-stability theorem and algebraic examples are part of \citet{smale1967dynamical}; the precise modern theorem is stated in \citet[Theorem 2.2]{spatzier2016rigidity}. The notebook itself correctly attributes the perturbation result to Anosov.

title: Lattice-preserving Lie-group automorphisms
notes: An automorphism of a Lie group preserves a discrete cocompact subgroup and descends to the quotient. It is \(U\) if its Lie-algebra map has no eigenvalue of modulus one.
statement: Let \(G\) be a simply connected Lie group with lattice \(\Gamma\), and let \(\Phi\in\operatorname{Aut}(G)\) satisfy \(\Phi(\Gamma)=\Gamma\). Its induced diffeomorphism of \(G/\Gamma\) is Anosov when \(d\Phi_e\) has no eigenvalue on the unit circle; the invariant tangent framing makes this criterion necessary as well. Nilpotent \(G\) gives the standard nilmanifold algebraic examples.
fate: The algebraic construction is described in \citet[algebraic examples]{smale1967dynamical} and is the model class in \citet[\S2]{spatzier2016rigidity}. The group, lattice-preservation, and compactness conditions are integral to the statement.
