reconstruction: This is an analytic local-isomorphism comparison; it is not an assertion that algebraic \(\acute{e}\)tale cohomology with arbitrary coefficients equals ordinary topology over every field.
fate: \citet[pp.~44--45]{mumford1965picard}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the comparison is established.

title: The site of families and cohomology of an individual family
notes: Objects are analytic families \(\pi:X\to S\), morphisms induce pullbacks, and covers are covers of bases. The cohomology of \(\pi\) is that of \(S\).
statement: For a fixed family \(\pi\), the local-isomorphism site of its pullbacks \(X\times_SU\to U\) is equivalent to the local-isomorphism site of \(S\). Thus a sheaf restricted to this slice has the corresponding cohomology \(H^q(S,F_\pi)\). Morphisms of families include a Cartesian square and its chosen fibrewise isomorphism.
reconstruction: The identification is for the slice over the particular family. It does not identify the cohomology of the entire moduli problem with the cohomology of one arbitrary base.
fate: The family-site construction is \citet[\S3]{mumford1965picard}; compare its induced-topology definition on p.~42.
present_status: As of November 2026, the slice comparison is established.

title: Products over the formal moduli object are isomorphism spaces
notes: The direct product of two families cannot simply have base \(S_1\times S_2\); the notes later count automorphisms as multiplicities. An earlier sentence says a curve's product with itself is itself.
statement: For proper smooth pointed genus-one families, or smooth proper curves of genus at least two, the product over the moduli object has base \(I=\operatorname{Isom}_{S_1\times S_2}(\operatorname{pr}_1^*X_1,\operatorname{pr}_2^*X_2)\). A point consists of \((s_1,s_2,\alpha)\) with \(\alpha:X_{1,s_1}\cong X_{2,s_2}\). Its fibre over \((s_1,s_2)\) is empty if the curves are nonisomorphic and otherwise a torsor under their automorphism group. A self-product therefore has one point for each automorphism, not necessarily one point.
reconstruction: The Isom space is an analytic space; smoothness or local biholomorphy requires additional conditions on the families. The lower-page multiplicity remark corrects the preceding set-level simplification.
fate: Exact construction in \citet[\S3, pp.~49--53]{mumford1965picard}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the Isom construction is established and retains the automorphism information lost by a coarse quotient.

title: Coverings of the formal terminal object
notes: A family \(\{\pi_i\to M\}\) covers if for every \(\pi\), the products \(\pi_i\times_M\pi\to\pi\) form a genuine covering. All families together need not be a covering.
statement: An atlas family covers the moduli object when every base change by an admissible family is represented by a jointly surjective family of local isomorphisms of bases. This requires both local deformation completeness and the appropriate unramified condition. Merely listing a representative of every curve, or including every possible family, does not ensure that each component map is eligible as an \(\acute{e}\)tale cover.
reconstruction: The covering class is fixed before applying joint surjectivity; adding non-\(\acute{e}\)tale families is not automatically permitted.
fate: \citet[\S3, pp.~50--54]{mumford1965picard}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the base-change test is established.

title: Analytic spaces are required for general fibre products
notes: The opening apology says that everywhere one should read analytic spaces, not analytic manifolds, because fibre products must exist.
statement: The category of complex analytic spaces admits fibre products of holomorphic maps. The subcategory of manifolds does not: the pullback of \(z\mapsto z^2\) along the map of a point to zero is the nonreduced analytic space with local ring \(\mathbb C\{z\}/(z^2)\). Even among reduced spaces, the equation \(x^2=y^2\) gives a singular pullback.
reconstruction: Nonreduced structure is retained in the first example; passing only to point sets would erase the obstruction. This is the lecturer's own correction, not a modern conjectural emendation.
fate: The distinction is already built into \citet[\S\S2--3]{mumford1965picard}. It corrects occurrence 1968-151.7.
present_status: As of November 2026, the category correction is established and necessary.

title: Fibre products and the three covering axioms repeated
notes: The universal square and its unique factorization are redrawn, followed by composition, identity and pullback of covers.
statement: For maps \(X\to Z\leftarrow Y\), \(X\times_ZY\) represents compatible pairs of maps into \(X,Y\). A pretopology has identity covers, composites of covering families as covers, and base-changed covers \(X_i\times_XY\to Y\). These statements include the existence of the indicated pullbacks.
reconstruction: The undeciphered letter above the self-map \(X\to X\) is understood as the identity map, as required by the axiom; no further mathematical content is assigned to the cancelled word.
fate: Already given in \citet[p.~38]{mumford1965picard}; this is a recurrence of 1967-143.1--1967-143.2 and 1968-151.1.
present_status: As of November 2026, the formulation is standard.

title: Abelian presheaves and effective gluing
notes: A presheaf is contravariant, and a sheaf has a unique global section inducing every compatible family of local sections.
statement: An abelian presheaf is a functor \(F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Ab}\). For each cover \(\{U_i\to U\}\), the map \(F(U)\to\prod_iF(U_i)\) identifies \(F(U)\) with the equalizer of the two restrictions to \(\prod_{i,j}F(U_i\times_UU_j)\). Thus compatibility is equality after the two projections, and both existence and uniqueness are required.
fate: \citet[p.~39]{mumford1965picard}; a repeated definition rather than an additional theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definition is established.

title: Canonical sheafification
notes: A parenthesis asserts a canonical procedure turning every presheaf into a sheaf for any topology.
statement: For a site, the inclusion of abelian sheaves into abelian presheaves has a left adjoint \(F\mapsto aF\), characterized by \(\operatorname{Hom}(aF,G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(F,G)\) for sheaves \(G\). For abelian groups sheafification is exact. In particular a presheaf may be nonzero while its associated sheaf vanishes because its sections vanish locally.
reconstruction: The universal property and exactness specify the construction used in the following comparison criterion; no claim that sections are unchanged is made.
fate: This is standard machinery in \citet[\S1]{mumford1965picard} and the sheaf-theoretic framework of \citet[\S3]{grothendieck1957homological}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is established.

title: Derived cohomology, exact sequences and injective acyclicity
notes: The notes prescribe \(H^0(U,F)=F(U)\), a long exact sequence for short exact sequences, enough injectives, and zero cohomology for injective sheaves.
statement: The category of abelian sheaves on a site has enough injectives. Deriving the left-exact sections functor gives \(H^q(U,F)\), with \(H^0(U,F)=F(U)\), functorial connecting morphisms, and the long exact cohomology sequence. An injective sheaf \(I\) has \(H^q(U,I)=0\) for \(q>0\); its degree-zero sections need not vanish.
reconstruction: The omitted positive-degree qualification is restored. Cohomology on \(U\) means cohomology in the slice site.
fate: \citet[pp.~37--39]{mumford1965picard}; \citet[\S\S2--3]{grothendieck1957homological}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected derived-functor assertions are established.

title: Local-acyclicity criterion for comparison of sites
notes: For a structure-compatible functor \(f:T_1\to T_2\), the notation \(f^*F(U)=F(f(U))\) is used. If the sheaf associated with \(U\mapsto H^i(f(U),F)\) is zero, the displayed cohomology map is an isomorphism.
statement: Let a functor \(u:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) induce a geometric morphism \(f:\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D)\to\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\) whose direct image is \(f_*F(U)=F(uU)\), and suppose the global-sections functors compose in the usual way. If \(R^if_*F=0\) for every \(i>0\), the Leray spectral sequence gives \(H^q(\mathcal C,f_*F)\cong H^q(\mathcal D,F)\). The higher direct image is computed by sheafifying the presheaf of cohomology over the inverse-image slices; when these are represented by \(uU\), this is \(U\mapsto H^i(\mathcal D/uU,F)\). The same criterion applies to the corresponding slices over an object.
reconstruction: The notebook's star labels precomposition, which is the direct-image functor for the geometric morphism in this convention. The positive-degree condition and the precise slice interpretation are supplied; a condition at \(i=0\) would generally force the coefficient sheaf itself to vanish.
fate: The exact application appears in \citet[\S7, p.~80, vanishing of \(R^iy_*\) for \(i>0\)]{mumford1965picard}; the homological argument is the Leray formalism of \citet[\S3]{grothendieck1957homological}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the criterion is established under the indicated functorial and acyclicity hypotheses.

title: A terminal moduli object and its candidate atlas
notes: A new category \(T_M\) adjoins a terminal object. Candidate covering families must contain every isomorphism type, with each type occurring only discretely.
statement: For a moduli category with representable isomorphism functors, an atlas is a family of objects whose maps to the moduli object are locally isomorphisms in the chosen topology and are jointly surjective after every base change. Meeting every isomorphism class is the pointwise-surjectivity part; discrete occurrence is a necessary unramified-type condition in this setting. Those two conditions alone do not prove local universality or the existence of the required pullbacks.
reconstruction: The local extension requirement on the next page supplies information beyond the two enumerated conditions. Formal adjunction of a terminal object is not treated as an existence proof for a fine moduli space.
fate: The precise modular-family construction is \citet[\S3, pp.~49--54]{mumford1965picard}; compare 1968-151.10--1968-151.11.
present_status: As of November 2026, the atlas construction is established for the stated moduli problem, with the local hypotheses retained.

title: Local extension property of a modular family
notes: A morphism from a subfamily over a submanifold is required to extend locally to a neighbourhood in the base of an arbitrary family; the picture calls it a tubular neighbourhood.
statement: A sufficient precise version is the following. Let \(X\to S\) be a modular analytic family such that, for every test family \(Y\to T\), its isomorphism space \(I=\operatorname{Isom}(Y,X)\to T\) is a local biholomorphism. A family morphism defined on an analytic subspace \(T_0\subset T\) gives a section of \(I\to T\) over \(T_0\). Near each point of \(T_0\), the inverse of the appropriate local biholomorphic branch extends that section, hence extends the family morphism.
reconstruction: This is a local assertion, not a global extension theorem or existence of a holomorphic tubular neighbourhood for every analytic subspace. The displayed crossed arrow does not uniquely encode a stronger formal deformation criterion.
fate: The isomorphism-space criterion and modular families are treated in \citet[\S3, pp.~50--54]{mumford1965picard}. The notebook gives an informal extension formulation of this mechanism.
present_status: As of November 2026, the precise local lifting statement is established; the broad tubular-neighbourhood wording needs the reconstruction above.

title: Resolving compatibility conditions for a differential system
notes: The Spencer resolution is presented as a method for solving \(p(x,D)u=w\), with a matrix \(p\) and vector-valued unknown and data.
statement: A differential operator \(P:\mathcal E\to\mathcal F\) of order \(\mu\) factors as \(\mathcal E\xrightarrow{j_\mu}J_\mu E\xrightarrow{p_\mu}F\). Prolonged equations and their compatibility operators yield Spencer complexes under constant-rank and regularity hypotheses. Their formal exactness is distinct from exactness on smooth sections. A locally exact compatibility complex gives local solvability for data satisfying its next compatibility equation; the unrestricted-jet resolution alone does not prove this for every \(P\).
reconstruction: The hypotheses are restored at the level of the method. Neither formal integrability nor the use of jets is presented as an unconditional smooth existence theorem.
fate: The expressly named source is \citet[Introduction; Chapter~I, \S3 and Proposition~8.3]{sweeney1968neumann}, received 4 September 1966, revised 30 November 1967, and printed June 1968. It gives exactness results for regular constant-coefficient systems and real-analytic germs under its stated hypotheses. Compare \citet[\S\S1.2,1.6]{spencer1969overdetermined}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the method and its specified applications are established; no general smooth-solvability claim follows from the note.

title: Finite jet bundles and an injective map of sheaves
notes: For the sheaf \(\mathcal O\) of smooth-function germs, \(j_\mu:\mathcal O\to J_\mu\) is said to be an embedding. The zeroth-order case is followed by an ambiguous zero symbol.
statement: On a smooth \(n\)-manifold, \(J_\mu\) is the vector bundle of \(\mu\)-jets of scalar functions. A local section of this bundle has coordinates \(\phi_I(x)\), \(0\le |I|\le\mu\), using unnormalized derivatives. Prolongation sends \(f\) to the section \(j_\mu f=(\partial^If)_I\). As a map of sheaves of real vector spaces it is injective because its zeroth component is \(f\). It is not the evaluation map from a function germ to its finite jet at one point, which is not injective. For \(\mu=0\), \(J_0\cong\mathcal O\) and \(j_0\) is the identity.
reconstruction: Bundles, sheaves of their sections, and individual jet fibres are distinguished. The subsequent map at order zero is to zero, yielding \(0\to\mathcal O\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}\mathcal O\to0\).
fate: \citet[Chapter~I, \S1 and Proposition~6.2]{sweeney1968neumann}; \citet[\S\S1.1,1.3]{spencer1969overdetermined}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction and sheaf-level injectivity are established.

title: Holonomic jet sections are characterized by derivative compatibility
notes: The notes first compare \(\partial\phi_0/\partial x_j\) with \(\phi_j\), then require \(\partial_j\phi_I=\phi_{I+1_j}\) for every \(|I|\le\mu-1\).
statement: A smooth local jet section \(\phi=(\phi_I)_{|I|\le\mu}\) is holonomic, meaning \(\phi=j_\mu f\) for a smooth function \(f\), if and only if \(\partial_j\phi_I=\phi_{I+e_j}\) for all \(j\) and \(|I|\le\mu-1\). Necessity follows by differentiation; sufficiency follows inductively from \(f=\phi_0\). For normalized Taylor coefficients the formula would instead contain the corresponding multi-index factors.
reconstruction: The derivative rather than Taylor-coefficient normalization is fixed by the first-order example. Gelfand's intervention is the coordinate presentation, not a separate conjecture.
fate: This is the kernel statement in \citet[Chapter~I, Proposition~5.1(ii)]{sweeney1968neumann} and \citet[equation~(1.3.2)]{spencer1969overdetermined}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the criterion is established and directly verified by induction.

title: The Spencer operator as actual minus formal differentiation
notes: The first operator is \(\sum_j(\partial_j\phi_I-\phi_{I+e_j})dx_j\), and its continuation is called \(D=d-\delta\).
statement: For a jet-valued differential form \(\phi\in\Omega^r\otimes J_k\), the Spencer operator is locally \((D\phi)_I=\sum_j dx_j\wedge(\partial_j\phi_I-\phi_{I+e_j})\), \(|I|\le k-1\). Thus \(D:\Omega^r\otimes J_k\to\Omega^{r+1}\otimes J_{k-1}\). It is a globally defined first-order differential operator; in these coordinates it is the difference of actual and formal exterior differentiation. The two summands separately depend on coordinates, whereas their difference does not.
reconstruction: The formula includes exterior degree, jet order, and the order of wedge factors. It is not linear over smooth functions for the usual module structures.
fate: \citet[Chapter~I, \S5, equation~(5.4)]{sweeney1968neumann}; \citet[equation~(1.3.1)\(^{\prime}\)]{spencer1969overdetermined}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the operator is established; its invariant character is essential to the resolution.

title: The one-form formula requires a wedge-order correction
notes: The displayed continuation is \(d(\phi_I^jdx_j)-\phi_{I+e_s}^jdx_j\wedge dx_s\), with the derivative-index correction also unclear.
statement:
With \(D=d-\delta\) as in the preceding degree-zero formula, the correct expression is 
\[
D(\phi_I^jdx_j)=\sum_{s,j}(\partial_s\phi_I^j-\phi_{I+e_s}^j)\,dx_s\wedge dx_j.
\]
Equivalently the formal term is \(+\sum_{s,j}\phi_{I+e_s}^jdx_j\wedge dx_s\). Retaining the printed minus sign together with the reversed wedge order is inconsistent with the previous definition and does not generally give \(D^2=0\).
reconstruction: The scan confirms the displayed order \(dx_j\wedge dx_s\); the choice \(e_s\) is dictated by the differentiation direction. The repair is mathematical, not a claim that the transcription omitted a legible sign.
fate: The corrected order is explicit in \citet[equation~(1.3.1)\(^{\prime}\)]{spencer1969overdetermined}; compare \citet[Chapter~I, equation~(5.4)]{sweeney1968neumann}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the literal sign-and-order combination is false; the corrected formula gives the standard differential.

title: The finite exact Spencer sequence for unrestricted jets
notes: The sequence \(\mathcal O\to J_\mu\to T^*\otimes J_{\mu-1}\to\Lambda^2T^*\otimes J_{\mu-2}\to\cdots\) is said to terminate and be exact.
statement:
For every \(\mu\ge0\), the sequence of sheaves of real vector spaces 
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal C^\infty_M\xrightarrow{j_\mu}J_\mu\xrightarrow D\Omega^1\otimes J_{\mu-1}\xrightarrow D\cdots\xrightarrow D\Omega^n\otimes J_{\mu-n}\longrightarrow0
\]
is exact, with \(J_k=0\) for \(k<0\). The identities \(d^2=\delta^2=0\) and \(d\delta+\delta d=0\) give \(D^2=0\); exactness follows inductively in jet order using the exact polynomial Koszul complex for the highest-order symbols. The same result holds for the jet bundle of any smooth vector bundle.
reconstruction: This resolves the sheaf of unrestricted smooth sections. For a subbundle of jets defined by a differential equation, exactness is a separate analytic issue, as explained in 1968-153.1. The individual maps are not morphisms of the usual smooth-function module structures.
fate: Exact publication match: \citet[Chapter~I, Proposition~6.2, p.~238]{sweeney1968neumann}; reproduced as equation~(1.3.3) with proof in \citet[\S1.3]{spencer1969overdetermined}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the finite jet resolution is established and was available before the seminar.

title: The unresolved comparison with a higher-order pseudo-object
notes: A marginal comparison reads either \ru{псевдогр.} or \ru{псевдооп.}, followed by ``one order higher''.
statement: No mathematical assertion beyond the legible jet construction can be uniquely recovered from this phrase. The first reading might refer to pseudogroups and the second to an operator construction, but the note does not supply a definition or a formula deciding between them.
reconstruction: Neither reading is silently promoted to an additional theorem; the names listed above it belong to the surrounding Spencer-theory attribution.
fate: \citet[Introduction and bibliography]{sweeney1968neumann} explicitly connects Spencer theory with pseudogroups, making that reading plausible but not conclusive. The alternative remains a transcription ambiguity.
present_status: As of November 2026, the marginal comparison remains unidentified; it is not an open mathematical problem.

title: Pointed elliptic families and Cartesian morphisms
notes: The objects are analytic families of complex tori with a distinguished section \(\sigma:S\to X\).
statement: An analytic family of pointed elliptic curves is a proper smooth holomorphic map \(\pi:E\to S\) with connected genus-one fibres, together with a holomorphic section \(e:S\to E\). Morphisms consist of a map of bases and a section-preserving isomorphism with the pulled-back family. The section makes each fibre an elliptic group curve and removes translation automorphisms, but retains the origin-preserving finite automorphisms.
reconstruction: Properness, smoothness and connected fibres specify the intended family category; arbitrary maps with pointwise torus fibres are not silently admitted.
fate: The category is the elliptic-curve case of \citet[\S4]{mumford1965picard}; see also \citet[\S2]{hain2008moduli}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the definition is established.

title: The coarse j-line has no smooth family realizing its identity parameter
notes: The quotient \(S'=\mathbb H/\Gamma\) is called coarse; the notes say there is a family with base \(S'\), then explain that the family over \(\mathbb H\) is not induced from it and that isotrivial twists are missed.
statement: For \(\Gamma=SL_2(\mathbb Z)\), the coarse quotient is the \(j\)-line. There is no smooth pointed elliptic family over the whole coarse line whose \(j\)-invariant is the identity. Locally near the square or hexagonal elliptic point, a family over a disc has a lifted period map to \(\mathbb H\); the coarse map is locally a square or cube of a local coordinate, so it cannot compose to a simple parameter on that disc. Separately, nontrivial isotrivial twists show that a pointwise classifying coarse map cannot classify all families.
reconstruction: The statement ``there is a family'' is false if it means one realizing each coarse parameter, as the surrounding discussion suggests. Trivial families over the line certainly exist but do not have the required classifying map. The two obstructions are distinguished.
fate: The exceptional local parameters are discussed in \citet[\S4, p.~59]{mumford1965picard}. The local lifting obstruction and isotrivial construction are explicit in \citet[Exercises~25--26, \S3.6]{hain2008moduli}. This repeats GP-1968-01.
present_status: As of November 2026, the coarse-versus-fine distinction and nonexistence are established.

title: The marked universal family and its modular action
notes: The family is \((\mathbb H\times\mathbb C)/((\tau,z)\sim(\tau,z+m\tau+n))\). The group acts by \(\tau'=(a\tau+b)/(c\tau+d)\), \(z'=z/(c\tau+d)\).
statement: The quotient \(\mathcal E_{\mathbb H}=(\mathbb H\times\mathbb C)/\mathbb Z^2\), with translations \(z\mapsto z+m\tau+n\), is a holomorphic family with zero section and a distinguished oriented homology basis. Every \(\gamma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in SL_2(\mathbb Z)\) lifts by the displayed formula because \((c\tau+d)^{-1}(\mathbb Z\tau+\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\gamma\tau+\mathbb Z\). The quotient family over the analytic stack \([\mathbb H/SL_2(\mathbb Z)]\) is universal in the family-category sense.
reconstruction: The notebook's underlined ``problem'' is the task of specifying this lifted action, answered on the next page; it is not a newly open problem. Stack notation is modern reconstruction.
fate: \citet[\S7]{mumford1965picard}; an explicit modern formulation is \citet[\S3.6, Theorem~3.18]{hain2008moduli}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction and action are established.

title: Three marked boundary points represent two exceptional orbits
notes: The fundamental-domain drawing marks three fixed points and says that branching occurs there.
statement: For the effective \(PSL_2(\mathbb Z)\)-action on \(\mathbb H\), there are two orbits with nontrivial stabilizers, represented by \(i\) and \(e^{2\pi i/3}\), with orders two and three. The two boundary representatives of the hexagonal orbit account for the third marked point in a closed fundamental domain. For \(SL_2(\mathbb Z)\), \(-I\) fixes every base point, so the generic stabilizer is \(C_2\), and the exceptional stabilizers are \(C_4,C_6\).
reconstruction: Counting points drawn in one closed domain is separated from counting orbits and from the non-effective central action.
fate: \citet[\S4]{mumford1965picard}; \citet[\S3.5, Example~3.14]{hain2008moduli}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stabilizer and branching descriptions are established after this qualification.

title: Constant coefficients and the cohomology of one family
notes: The coefficient sheaf has one copy of \(\mathbb Z\) for each connected component, and \(H^q(\pi,\mathbb Z)=H^q(S,\mathbb Z)\).
statement: On the local-isomorphism slice over a family \(\pi:E\to S\), the constant coefficient sheaf assigns locally constant integer-valued functions to each base. If a base \(U\) is locally connected, this group is \(\prod_{\pi_0(U)}\mathbb Z\). The slice-site comparison identifies \(H^q(\pi,\mathbb Z)\) with ordinary sheaf cohomology \(H^q(S,\mathbb Z)\). These are not the cohomology groups of the total space \(E\), nor yet those of the terminal moduli object.
reconstruction: The finite three-summand drawing is harmless; for an infinite set of components one must take a product. Connected components are open for the analytic spaces under discussion.
fate: The comparison uses \citet[\S\S2--3]{mumford1965picard} and repeats 1968-151.8--1968-151.9 with specified coefficients.
present_status: As of November 2026, the slice identification is established.

title: The level-three subsite and comparison with group cohomology
notes: A subcategory of \(\Gamma\)-sets has point stabilizers inside \(\Gamma_3\). The assignment \(S\mapsto(\mathbb H\times S)/\Gamma\) induces a cohomology isomorphism after adjoining terminal objects.
statement: Let \(\Gamma=SL_2(\mathbb Z)\) and \(\Gamma(3)=\ker(\Gamma\to SL_2(\mathbb Z/3))\). This subgroup is torsion-free. For a discrete \(\Gamma\)-set \(S\) with all stabilizers contained in \(\Gamma(3)\), the diagonal action on \(\mathbb H\times S\) is free and its quotient is a complex analytic base carrying the descended elliptic family. These objects form the comparison subsite. Contractibility of \(\mathbb H\), local acyclicity and the covering criterion give \(H^q(\mathcal M_{1,1}^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb Z)\cong H^q(\Gamma,\mathbb Z)\).
reconstruction: The freeness is for the diagonal action on these admissible objects; the full modular action on the upper half-plane is not free. The formal terminal object is adjoined because the one-point \(\Gamma\)-set does not satisfy the stabilizer restriction.
fate: Exact construction and comparison: \citet[\S7, pp.~79--80]{mumford1965picard}. The classifying-space interpretation is \citet[Proposition~3.13]{hain2008moduli}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the comparison is established.

title: Integral cohomology of the elliptic moduli site is periodic
notes: The formula is transcribed as \(H^q(M,\mathbb Z)=0\) for \(q\ne2\), and \(\mathbb Z_{12}\) for \(q=2\); the degree sign is heavily retraced.
statement:
For the uncompactified analytic moduli stack of pointed elliptic curves,
\[
H^q(\mathcal M_{1,1}^{\mathrm{an}},\mathbb Z)=
\begin{cases}\mathbb Z,&q=0,\\\mathbb Z/12,&q>0\text{ even},\\0,&q\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
\]
More precisely its ring is \(\mathbb Z[c]/(12c)\), with \(|c|=2\). This differs both from the coarse \(j\)-line, whose positive-degree integral cohomology vanishes, and from the compactified moduli stack.
reconstruction: The higher-degree correction follows from \(SL_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_4*_{C_2}C_6\). In every positive even degree the Mayer--Vietoris map \(\mathbb Z/4\oplus\mathbb Z/6\to\mathbb Z/2\) is \((a,b)\mapsto a-b\) modulo two, is surjective, and has cyclic kernel of order twelve. The odd groups vanish; degree zero is \(\mathbb Z\). Choosing the degree-two class restricting to generators of both cyclic groups gives the displayed ring. This is an explicit verification of a correction, not a novel cohomology theorem.
fate: The moduli-to-group comparison is \citet[\S7]{mumford1965picard}; the degree-one and degree-two computation and group presentation are in \citet[Proposition~3.13 and presentation~(3)]{hain2008moduli}. The periodic extension is verified by the amalgam calculation above.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected integral cohomology is established; the literal concentration in degree two is false.

title: The assertion over other fields concerns the Picard group
notes: The notes say that the answer remains true over any field of characteristic different from two.
statement: For every field \(k\), the algebraic Picard group of the stack of elliptic curves is \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal M_{1,1,k})\cong\mathbb Z/12\), generated by the Hodge line bundle. This is a statement about invertible sheaves. Ordinary integral Betti cohomology is the complex-analytic invariant of the preceding item and is not defined by that formula for an arbitrary field.
reconstruction: The text switches invariants without explaining the comparison. Mumford's theorem as published assumes characteristic different from both two and three. Its Picard conclusion over fields of characteristic three, and indeed two, has a later exact extension; this does not extend the entire displayed Betti-cohomology table to all fields.
fate: \citet[\S6, Main Theorem, p.~73]{mumford1965picard} proves the characteristic-not-two-or-three case. \citet[Theorem~1.1]{fultonolsson2010picard}, circulated on 17 April 2007 and published in 2010, proves \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal M_{1,1,S})\cong\mathbb Z/12\oplus\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb A^1_S)\) for reduced \(S\), or when two is invertible on \(S\). For \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\), the second summand is zero.
present_status: As of November 2026, the algebraic Picard assertion is established for every field. The literal general-field cohomology statement is under-specified until its invariant and topology are fixed.

title: What the invariant modulo twelve means for a family
notes: A boxed conclusion says that families have an invariant modulo twelve.
statement: The universal Hodge line bundle \(\lambda\) generates the cyclic Picard group of order twelve. For a smooth pointed elliptic family \(\pi:E\to S\), its pullback is \(\lambda_S=\pi_*\Omega^1_{E/S}\), and the nonvanishing discriminant gives a canonical trivialization of \(\lambda_S^{\otimes12}\). In the complex analytic setting, \(c_1(\lambda_S)\in H^2(S,\mathbb Z)\) is the pullback of the universal order-twelve class and is killed by twelve.
reconstruction: A family over an arbitrary base does not automatically yield a scalar in \(\mathbb Z/12\). It yields a line-bundle class, or its cohomology class on that base, whose universal source has order twelve.
fate: \citet[\S6]{mumford1965picard}; \citet[Introduction, equations~(1-3)--(1-7)]{fultonolsson2010picard}; the analytic generator is \citet[Theorem~6.6]{hain2008moduli}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the Hodge-line interpretation and its order-twelve relation are established.

title: Shafarevich: a site of transverse patches and holonomy
notes: For an ordinary differential equation, objects are transverse patches and maps follow trajectories to another patch. A fibre product is drawn.
statement: For a nonsingular smooth foliation, choose a complete transversal \(T\). Germs of holonomy maps between open subsets of \(T\) form an \(\acute{e}\)tale groupoid \(G\). Equivariant sheaves on \(T\), or the corresponding local site with ordinary open covers and holonomy identifications, retain the transverse topology and isotropy of the foliation. Fibre products of local transverse maps exist locally after restricting patches. Singular points require an additional definition and are not covered by this nonsingular construction.
reconstruction: The holonomy-groupoid interpretation makes the drawing precise but is a modern reconstruction. The note does not say whether path data, holonomy germs or only pointwise trajectory incidence define its morphisms; those choices can produce different groupoids.
fate: A precise later development is \citet[\S\S1.1,2.1--2.2 and Theorem~3.1]{moerdijk1991foliations}: the classifying topos of an \(\acute{e}\)tale groupoid agrees in homotopy and cohomology with its classifying space. This matches the transverse-site method, not the unqualified singular-flow or Euler formula in the next remarks. The paper appeared in 1991; no earlier circulation date was verified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the nonsingular holonomy-site construction is established; the exact morphism convention of this notebook example remains only partially identified.
speaker: I. R. Shafarevich

title: For a genuine leaf fibration the transverse cohomology is that of the base
notes: The abbreviated sentence says that, for a fibration, the cohomology of the base and the system are \ru{трив.}, and mentions a final object.
statement: If a foliation is the foliation by connected fibres of a surjective smooth submersion \(p:M\to B\) with manifold leaf space \(B\), its holonomy groupoid on a complete transversal is equivalent to the \(\acute{e}\)tale groupoid presenting \(B\). Its classifying topos is therefore equivalent to ordinary sheaves on \(B\), and the corresponding cohomology groups agree. They need not vanish: a nonempty connected base has \(H^0(B,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\).
reconstruction: The abbreviation may mean that the identification is trivial, rather than that both cohomologies vanish. The Russian and scan do not decide the omitted predicate. The existence of a terminal object by itself never forces positive-degree cohomology to vanish.
fate: The groupoid invariance is \citet[\S2.2]{moerdijk1991foliations}; for a groupoid presenting a space the classifying topos is its usual sheaf topos, as explained in \S2.4 of that paper. The fibration case follows directly.
present_status: As of November 2026, the base comparison is established; a reading asserting vanishing is false and the notebook wording remains ambiguous.
speaker: I. R. Shafarevich

title: Euler characteristic as a difference of cycle and singular-point counts
notes: For an equation on the plane and the constant sheaf of its Grothendieck topology, the Euler characteristic is said to be the difference between the number of limit cycles and the number of singular points.
statement: No precise theorem is determined without specifying the vector-field class, treatment of singular leaves, cohomology theory and support condition, finiteness of the relevant groups, and which signed difference is intended. For example, for the constant nonzero horizontal vector field on \(\mathbb R^2\), the ordinary transverse leaf space is \(\mathbb R\), with ordinary constant-sheaf Euler characteristic one, while both stated counts are zero. Thus the unrestricted ordinary-cohomology interpretation is false.
reconstruction: The counterexample does not identify the author's intended compact-support, reduced or relative invariant. It demonstrates why the omitted convention is substantive. The phrase does not supply a definite open problem, and no problem-index entry is invented.
fate: Searches combining the named speaker, transverse sites, Euler characteristic, singular points and limit cycles did not identify a publication with these exact hypotheses and conclusion. \citet[Theorem~3.1]{moerdijk1991foliations} provides the general cohomological framework but no such cycle-count formula.
present_status: As of November 2026, the intended invariant and theorem remain unidentified; the broad ordinary-cohomology reading is refuted by the stated elementary example.
speaker: I. R. Shafarevich

title: Hyperbolic uniformization and unramified coverings
notes: \(X=\Gamma\backslash M\), with \(M\) the Lobachevsky plane; \(\Gamma\) describes both \(X\) and its unramified coverings.
statement: For a torsion-free discrete subgroup \(\Gamma<\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\), the projection \(\mathbb H\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H\) is a universal covering. Connected coverings correspond, up to isomorphism, to conjugacy classes of subgroups of \(\Gamma\); finite covers correspond to finite-index subgroups. Compact Riemann surfaces of genus at least two admit such uniformization.
reconstruction: Torsion-freeness, connectedness, genus restriction, and conjugacy of subgroups make the notebook shorthand precise.
fate: This is Ihara\textquoteright s classical starting analogy, not his new finite-field correspondence \citep[Introduction]{ihara1968monodromy}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Coordinate rings, closed points, and contravariance
notes: \(A=k[x,y]/(f)\); maximal ideals are called geometric points, and \(Y\to X\) induces \(A\to B\).
statement: For an affine plane curve \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[x,y]/(f))\), closed points correspond to maximal ideals, while \(\bar k\)-valued geometric points are homomorphisms \(A\to\bar k\). An affine morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is equivalent to a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism \(A\to B\). A closed point may have several geometric points above it.
fate: Pre-existing algebraic geometry used in Ihara\textquoteright s finite-field setting \citep[\S0]{ihara1968monodromy}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Reduced fibres as a criterion for unramifiedness
notes: For a maximal ideal \(m\subset A\), if \(B/mB\) has no nilpotents, the map is unramified at \(m\).
statement: For a finite morphism of finite-type schemes over a perfect field, at a closed point \(x\) the morphism is unramified at every point above \(x\) if and only if its fibre algebra is a finite product of finite separable extensions of \(\kappa(x)\). Over finite fields the residue field is perfect, so reducedness of that finite fibre algebra suffices. Flatness is an additional condition for an \emph{\'{e}tale} morphism.
reconstruction: Finiteness and separability are supplied. A reduced fibre over an imperfect field need not be unramified.
fate: The finite unramified extensions are the objects of Ihara\textquoteright s Conjecture 2; the fibre test is older background \citep[p.~107]{ihara1968monodromy}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Jet bundles and holonomic jet sections
notes: \(O\hookrightarrow J^k\); a jet is a family \(\{\varphi_i:|i|\leq k\}\) transforming like derivatives.
statement: For a smooth manifold \(X\), \(J^k(X,\mathbb R)_x\) consists of germs of smooth functions at \(x\) modulo equality of all derivatives through order \(k\). The map \(j^k:C^\infty_X\to\mathcal J^k\) sends a function to its jet section. It is injective as a map of sheaves of real vector spaces, but is not \(C^\infty_X\)-linear for the usual module structure on jet sections.
reconstruction: The sheaf consists of arbitrary smooth sections of the jet bundle; holonomic sections are the image of the jet map.
fate: The construction is explained in \citet[Chapter~I, \S1]{sweeney1968neumann}, published before this October talk.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Jets from a power of the diagonal ideal
notes: \(\varphi_1\sim\varphi_2\) when \(\varphi_1-\varphi_2\in\mathcal J^{k+1}\), with \(\mathcal J\) the ideal of functions vanishing on the diagonal of \(X\times X\).
statement: Let \(\mathcal I_\Delta\) be the sheaf of smooth functions vanishing on the diagonal. The sheaf \(C^\infty_{X\times X}/\mathcal I_\Delta^{k+1}\), restricted to a neighbourhood germ of \(\Delta\) and viewed over the first projection, is the sheaf of order-\(k\) jets in the second variable. Locally its elements are finite Taylor polynomials in \(y-x\).
reconstruction: The choice of projection and the germ along the diagonal are supplied; the two projections yield two module structures.
fate: This is the principal-parts description of the jets used in \citet[Chapter~I, \S1]{sweeney1968neumann}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Many-point jets and the first-order splitting
notes: Gelfand replaces \(X\times X\) by \(X^{m+1}\), uses the small diagonal, and says \((1,m)\)-jet equals a scalar function plus a differential form.
statement: With the first factor distinguished, \(C^\infty_{X^{m+1}}/\mathcal I_\Delta^{k+1}\) records total normal Taylor degree at most \(k\). Its first-order part is \(C^\infty_X\oplus (T^*X)^{\oplus m}\) as a module: one scalar and \(m\) covectors. For \(m=1,k=1\) this is a function plus one one-form. The displayed \((1,m)\) wording does not describe a general higher jet.
reconstruction: The normal bundle of the small diagonal and its chosen first-factor splitting give the precise interpretation; no antisymmetrization is specified in the notes.
fate: The two-point case is standard jet theory \citep[Chapter~I, \S1]{sweeney1968neumann}; the many-point notation is a notebook reformulation.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Two Taylor descriptions of a first jet
notes: \(\varphi(x,y)=\varphi(x,x)+\partial_x\varphi|_{y=x}(y-x)\), followed by the analogous expression with \(x,y\) reversed.
statement: Modulo \(\mathcal I_\Delta^2\), the correct formula with \(x\) fixed is \(\varphi(x,y)=\varphi(x,x)+\partial_y\varphi(x,x)(y-x)\); with \(y\) fixed it is \(\varphi(x,y)=\varphi(y,y)+\partial_x\varphi(y,y)(x-y)\). Both are identities of first-order jets, not exact equalities of arbitrary smooth functions.
reconstruction: Equality is interpreted modulo the squared diagonal ideal, and the differentiated variables are corrected.
fate: Ordinary Taylor expansion; the scan confirms the derivative variables were interchanged in the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The trivial Spencer resolution
notes: \(0\to O_X\xrightarrow{j}J^k\xrightarrow{d_x}T^*\otimes J^{k-1}\xrightarrow{d_x}\Lambda^2T^*\otimes J^{k-2}\to\cdots\), called the trivial Spencer resolution.
statement: For the trivial scalar equation, the Spencer operator is \((D\sigma)_\alpha=d\sigma_\alpha-\sum_i\sigma_{\alpha+e_i}\,dx_i\), \(|\alpha|<k\). It extends to forms, satisfies \(D^2=0\), and the sheaf sequence \(0\to C^\infty_X\xrightarrow{j^k}\mathcal J^k\xrightarrow D\Lambda^1T^*X\otimes\mathcal J^{k-1}\xrightarrow D\cdots\xrightarrow D\Lambda^nT^*X\otimes\mathcal J^{k-n}\to0\) is exact, interpreting negative-order jet terms as zero.
reconstruction: The Spencer differential is distinguished from componentwise exterior differentiation, and the negative-order terms are set to zero as in the cited proposition.
fate: Exactly \citet[Chapter~I, Proposition~6.2, p.~238]{sweeney1968neumann}, published before the talk. The quotient construction for the second Spencer sequence is a separate construction and is unnecessary in this displayed first sequence.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Extension from trivial jets to linear PDE systems
notes: Replace \(O_X\) by the sheaf of solutions of an arbitrary linear system. Sweeney, Malgrange, Quillen are named.
statement: For a linear differential operator one forms prolonged equation bundles and their Spencer complexes. Formal integrability, regularity of the prolongations, and appropriate local exactness hypotheses are needed before the complex resolves the solution sheaf. An arbitrary linear system does not automatically inherit the exact trivial complex.
reconstruction: This gives a precise conditional method, not an assertion of local solvability for every smooth system.
fate: \citet[Chapter~I, \S\S7--8]{sweeney1968neumann} separates stability and exactness; the other two notebook references remain unspecified.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Operator-valued integral kernels
notes: \(\mathcal Kf(x)=\int_MK(x,y)f(y)\,d\mu(y)\) on \(L^2(M,H)\), with a Hilbert space or Hermitian bundle and weak joint continuity.
statement: Let \(M\) be a compact smooth manifold with a finite smooth positive measure and \(H\) a separable Hilbert space. A jointly weakly continuous kernel \(K:M^2\to\mathcal B(H)\) is uniformly bounded and determines a bounded integral operator on \(L^2(M,H)\). The same construction works in finite-rank Hermitian bundles using fibre maps.
reconstruction: A finite smooth measure, separability, and the distinction between weak continuity and trace-norm continuity are supplied.
fate: The setup is exactly that of \citet[Lemma~8]{kirillov1968characters}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Diagonal trace formula and positive converse
notes: \(\operatorname{tr}\mathcal K=\int_M\operatorname{tr}K(x,x)d\mu(x)\). Existence of the right-hand side is necessary, and for positive operators sufficient.
statement: Under the preceding kernel hypotheses, if \(\mathcal K\) is trace class then \(K(x,x)\) is trace class almost everywhere, the diagonal trace is integrable, and the displayed equality holds. If \(\mathcal K\geq0\), almost-everywhere existence of the diagonal trace together with its finite integral also implies that \(\mathcal K\) is trace class.
fate: Already proved in \citet[Lemma~8, Russian pp.~49--50]{kirillov1968characters}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Why the almost-everywhere diagonal statement matters
notes: The nontrivial point is that trace class of \(\mathcal K\) implies existence of \(\operatorname{tr}K(x,x)\) almost everywhere; scalar kernels are referred to Gohberg--Krein and Carleman.
statement: The trace-class condition concerns an operator on \(L^2(M,H)\), not pointwise operators on \(H\). Weak continuity and the integral representation bridge those two levels. Without a regular representative of a merely measurable kernel, its values on the diagonal can be changed arbitrarily on a product-measure null set, so a naive diagonal formula has no invariant meaning.
reconstruction: The measurable-kernel caution explains the role of the recorded continuity hypothesis; it is not a new open problem.
fate: Kirillov\textquoteright s Lemma~8 proves this distinction rather than assuming pointwise trace class \citep{kirillov1968characters}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Rayleigh quotients and constrained extrema
notes: \(R(u)=(Au,u)/(u,u)\), followed by an Euler equation and the constraint \(u\perp\mathcal P_n\).
statement: For a densely defined semibounded self-adjoint operator \(A\) with compact resolvent, the Rayleigh quotient is minimized on the unit sphere of its form domain. The unconstrained Euler equation is \(Au=\lambda u\); with constraints \(u\perp p_j\), it becomes \((A-\lambda)u=\sum_jc_jp_j\). The min--max principle characterizes the discrete eigenvalues.
reconstruction: Semiboundedness, form domains, compact resolvent, and Lagrange multipliers make the variational statement precise.
fate: The Rayleigh and constrained-minimum formulation occurs in \citet[\S\S1--2; Russian translation pp.~91--93]{weinstein1963intermediate}, predating the talk.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Finite constraint determinants and intermediate lower bounds
notes: \(\mathcal P=\bigcup_n\mathcal P_n\); minimizing on \(u\perp\mathcal P_n\) gives a determinant equation. Classical bounds come from one side, Weinstein\textquoteright s from the other.
statement: For \(\lambda\notin\sigma(A)\), constrained eigenvalues may be detected by the finite matrix \(G_{ij}(\lambda)=\langle(A-\lambda)^{-1}p_j,p_i\rangle\), through \(\det G(\lambda)=0\). Persistent eigenvalues in \(\sigma(A)\) need separate treatment. In intermediate-problem methods one chooses ordered, explicitly tractable quadratic forms converging to the target; their min--max eigenvalues give certified bounds, with convergence requiring density in the relevant form norm.
reconstruction: The resolvent determinant is an explicit reconstruction of the ellipsis, valid only off the original spectrum; it is not a recovered formula.
fate: \citet[\S\S2--4]{weinstein1963intermediate} treats the generalized intermediate problems and their meromorphic spectral functions. The specific finite-matrix display fills the notebook ellipsis and is labeled reconstruction.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Extension to Schrödinger operators
notes: The constrained minimum exists for the Schrödinger operator, not only for completely continuous operators.
statement: For a semibounded self-adjoint Schrödinger operator, min--max values below the essential spectrum are discrete eigenvalues and are attained when they lie strictly below its bottom. Compact resolvent is one sufficient global condition. An arbitrary Schrödinger operator on a noncompact domain need not attain the infimum of its Rayleigh quotient.
reconstruction: Spectral isolation or compactness is essential; the notes do not specify a potential or domain.
fate: The operator formulation belongs to the classical intermediate-problem framework \citep{weinstein1963intermediate}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The Rolewicz periodic delay-equation notice
notes: An unnamed Pole, written Rolevich, discusses periodic solutions of delay equations, reduction to ordinary equations with periodic coefficients, and control applications.
statement: No delay length, equation, phase space, regularity, periodicity relation, or reduction map is specified. The strongest faithful statement is a programme notice about such a reduction; a general equivalence between delay equations and finite-dimensional ODEs would be false.
reconstruction: Rolevich plausibly refers to Stefan Rolewicz; the matching literature also includes Danuta Przeworska-Rolewicz. No first name is supplied by the source.

They support the programme identification but do not establish the exact reduction or which author spoke.

title: Distribution characters and their test-function domain
notes: \(T(\varphi)=\int_G\varphi(g)T(g)\,dg\); if its trace exists, \(\operatorname{tr}T(\varphi)=\langle\chi,\varphi\rangle\). The examples appear no worse than measures, but no general theorem is asserted.
statement: For a strongly continuous unitary representation \(\pi\) of a Lie group with a fixed left Haar measure, \(\pi(\varphi)\) is bounded for \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(G)\). title: Extracting the polynomial square root of a skew determinant
notes: Problem: for a skew-symmetric matrix, extract a polynomial square root of its determinant; the two-by-two example is given as \(-a^2\).

title: Hypoellipticity and the second-order class
notes: \(Pu=a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu\); hypoelliptic is followed by a question mark.
statement: On an open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\), a differential operator \(P\) with smooth coefficients is hypoelliptic if for every open \(U\subset\Omega\) and every distribution \(u\in\mathcal D^{\prime}(U)\), \(Pu\in C^\infty(U)\) implies \(u\in C^\infty(U)\). The announced real second-order results concern a symmetric nonnegative principal matrix \((a^{ij})\), not arbitrary complex principal forms.
reconstruction: Distributional and local quantifiers, smoothness, and the nonnegative form are supplied.
fate: The definition and coefficient class are explicit in \citet[pp.~139--140]{oleinikradkevich1971local}; H\"ormander\textquoteright s preceding result supplies the comparison class.

title: Hörmander brackets imply hypoellipticity and a positive Sobolev gain
notes: For \(P=\sum X_i^2+X_0+c\), if at every point there are \(n\) independent commutators then \(P\) is hypoelliptic, using \(\|u\|_\varepsilon\le C(\|u\|_0+\|Pu\|_0)\), \(\varepsilon>0\).
statement: Let \(X_0,\ldots,X_r\) be smooth real vector fields on \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\), and \(c\) smooth. If their iterated Lie brackets span \(T_x\Omega\) at every point, then \(P=\sum_{j=1}^rX_j^2+X_0+c\) is hypoelliptic. For each compact \(K\Subset\Omega\), there are \(C,\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\|u\|_{H^\varepsilon}\le C(\|Pu\|_{L^2}+\|u\|_{L^2})\) for \(u\in C_c^\infty(K)\); localized higher-order estimates yield smoothness.
fate: Already \citet[Theorem~1.1 and its proof]{hormander1967hypoelliptic}, in the 1967 volume (printed February 1968). Radkevich\textquoteright s revised estimates appeared as \citet[Theorems~1,3]{radkevich1969hormander}.

These are different assertions. Hypoellipticity with smooth coefficients cannot in general be characterized solely by the rank of the vector-field family.

title: An elliptic commutator system built from symbol derivatives
notes: Use \(P^{(j)}=a^{ij}D_i\) and \(P_{(j)}=\sum\partial_{x_j}a_{ik}\,\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_k}\,\mathcal E_{-1}\); retain principal parts and their commutators until an elliptic system is obtained.
statement: Let \(L=\sum a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+\sum b^i\partial_i+c\) have real smooth coefficients and symmetric nonnegative matrix \(a\). Put \(p(x,\xi)=\sum a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j\) and let \(Q\) be the first-order drift in the divergence-form rewriting. Form first-order pseudodifferential operators with principal symbols \(\partial_{\xi_j}p\) and \(|\xi|^{-1}\partial_{x_j}p\), together with \(Q\). Suppose on every compact \(K\Subset\Omega\) finitely many of their iterated commutators have principal symbols \(q_J\) satisfying \(\sum_J|q_J(x,\xi)|^2\ge c_K|\xi|^2\) for \(x\in K, |\xi|\ge1\). Then \(L\) is hypoelliptic and has localized positive-gain estimates.
reconstruction: The drift term, nonnegative characteristic form, finite uniform ellipticity on compacts, and the normalization of symbol derivatives are taken from the published formulation. The notes omit these details.
fate: The completed criterion is \citet[Theorem~6, pp.~145--147]{oleinikradkevich1971local}; the 1969 announcements are listed there as references~14--16. The original two-page \citet[Theorems~2--3]{radkevich1969hormander} proves a related general commutator criterion.

title: Toward a formulation containing Hörmander’s theorem
notes: There is as yet no formulation including H\"ormander\textquoteright s theorem; the first-order case should work without pseudodifferential operators.
statement: The programme is to place vector-field sum-of-squares estimates and general second-order nonnegative-form estimates in a common commutator framework. For differential first-order generators, brackets remain differential; derivative-of-symbol operators normalized by order-minus-one factors generally require pseudodifferential calculus.

title: When are all generalized solutions locally integrable?
notes: Gelfand: for applications it is important to know when every solution is a summable function.
statement: One possible precise property is \(\ker(P:\mathcal D^{\prime}(U)\to\mathcal D^{\prime}(U))\subset L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)\) for every open \(U\). Hypoellipticity implies it, but the notebook does not specify homogeneous versus inhomogeneous equations, the allowed right-hand sides, or which coefficient class is to be characterized. Global integrability would be a different condition.

title: Scheme points, closed points, and geometric points
notes: \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak J\); maximal ideals give closed points, prime ideals give points; \(A/I\) is a finite extension of \(k\). A map \(A\to K\) is called a geometric point.
statement: For a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra \(A\), points of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) are prime ideals and closed points are maximal ideals. Zariski\textquoteright s lemma says that the residue field at a maximal ideal is finite over \(k\). A geometric point is a morphism from the spectrum of an algebraically closed field; a homomorphism to an arbitrary field is a field-valued point, whose kernel need not be maximal if the field extension is transcendental. For \(\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)\), one closed point yields two \(\mathbb C\)-valued points.
reconstruction: The residue-field finiteness assertion is restricted to closed points, and geometric versus arbitrary field-valued points is distinguished.
fate: This is pre-existing background for the closed-point definition used by \citet[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}. It also corrects the shorthand at record155.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Reduced schemes and the word variety
notes: An algebraic variety is distinguished from a scheme by absence of nilpotent elements.
statement: An affine scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) is reduced precisely when \(A\) has no nonzero nilpotents. A variety has additional convention-dependent hypotheses, commonly finite type, separatedness, and sometimes irreducibility. Reducedness alone is not a definition of an arbitrary variety. Finite-field point counts and the associated zeta function are unchanged by passage to the reduction.
reconstruction: The source\textquoteright s local terminology is translated into the precise property reduced, without imposing one universal convention for variety.
fate: Dwork\textquoteright s zeta function counts field-valued points \citep[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}; maps to fields kill nilpotents, which explains this last assertion directly.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Finite fields and Frobenius
notes: \(\mathbb F_{p^n}\) is obtained by a displayed polynomial with overwritten exponents; its automorphism group is cyclic, generated by \(x\mapsto x^p\).
statement: Inside an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_p\), the roots of \(X^{p^n}-X\) form the unique field of cardinality \(p^n\). Its Galois group over \(\mathbb F_p\) is cyclic of order \(n\), generated by Frobenius. To present this field as a quotient of \(\mathbb F_p[X]\), one chooses an irreducible polynomial of degree \(n\); the entire polynomial \(X^{p^n}-X\) does not define a field quotient when \(n>1\).
reconstruction: A correct root-set construction is supplied independently of the unreadable fraction; it is not offered as a recovered reading.
fate: This is the elementary finite-field structure used throughout \citet[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}. The corrupted displayed quotient cannot be certified as a defining polynomial.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The closed-point Euler product
notes: Degree of a closed point is its residue-field degree; \(\zeta(t,A)=\prod_x(1-t^{\deg x})^{-1}\), with \(t\) formal.
statement: For a finite-type scheme \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(|X|\) be its set of closed points and \(\deg x=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\). Then \(Z(X,t)=\prod_{x\in|X|}(1-t^{\deg x})^{-1}\in1+t\mathbb Z[[t]]\). Finitely many closed points have each bounded degree, so each coefficient is a finite sum. The product is initially formal, without a claim of convergence on the complex unit circle.
fate: This is Dwork\textquoteright s input zeta function \citep[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Dwork rationality
notes: For every affine algebraic variety over a finite field the Euler product is rational; this was a Weil conjecture and was known earlier for curves.
statement: For every finite-type scheme \(X/\mathbb F_q\), \(Z(X,t)\) is the Taylor expansion at zero of an element of \(\mathbb Q(t)\). The affine statement extends by finite stratification and multiplicativity for disjoint locally closed strata; nilpotents do not affect point counts. This is the rationality part, not the entire collection of Weil conjectures.
reconstruction: The finite-type scheme extension is explained; no purity, functional-equation, or Riemann-hypothesis conclusion is attributed to Dwork\textquoteright s rationality theorem.
fate: Established before the talk by \citet[main theorem]{dwork1960rationality}, published in 1960; the Russian translation appeared in 1961.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Affine-line closed points and irreducible-polynomial counts
notes: For \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), \(Z=1/(1-pt)\), and the degree-one, two, three, four factors have exponents \(p,(p^2-p)/2,(p^3-p)/3,(p^4-p^2)/4\).
statement: The number of degree-\(d\) closed points of \(\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb F_q}\) is \(b_d=d^{-1}\sum_{e\mid d}\mu(e)q^{d/e}\). Indeed \(q^r=\sum_{d\mid r}db_d\), because a degree-\(d\) closed point contributes \(d\) points over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\) exactly when \(d\mid r\). Thus \(Z(\mathbb A^1,t)=(1-qt)^{-1}\). Every displayed Euler factor should have negative exponent in the product.
reconstruction: The general degree formula is derived from Frobenius orbits; the fourth factor is interpreted as a denominator like the preceding factors.
fate: The example is pre-existing elementary finite-field counting, consistent with \citet[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}; M\"obius inversion fills the notebook\textquoteright s omitted general expression.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Poles of formal Euler factors are not poles of the continued zeta function
notes: After \(Z(\mathbb A^1,t)=1/(1-pt)\), the note says the infinite expansion has poles at one.
statement: Each Euler factor \((1-t^d)^{-1}\) has poles at roots of unity, including one. The infinite product for the affine line is initially convergent only for \(|t|<1/q\), and its rational continuation has its sole pole at \(t=1/q\). Poles of individual factors outside the convergence region cannot be read as poles of that continuation.
reconstruction: The unclear scope of poles at one is interpreted as a comment on the individual factors, not silently attributed to the rational function.
fate: The affine-line identity in the notebook itself resolves the distinction; the formal/analytic separation is consistent with \citet[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Uniqueness of formal Euler factorization
notes: Uniqueness? The degree is chosen at the last possible step to match a coefficient; hence every series can be expanded.
statement: Every series \(F(t)\in1+t\mathbb Z[[t]]\) has a unique formal expansion \(F(t)=\prod_{n\ge1}(1-t^n)^{-b_n}\) with \(b_n\in\mathbb Z\). Choose \(b_n\) recursively to cancel the coefficient of \(t^n\) after the earlier factors are removed; uniqueness follows from the first degree at which two sequences differ. The exponents need not be nonnegative, so an arbitrary such series need not be the zeta function of a variety.
reconstruction: The coefficient ring, constant term, allowance of negative exponents, and formal-product meaning are supplied.
fate: The notebook itself gives the recursive method. This is a solved formal-algebra exercise in the exposition and receives no new historical problem identifier.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The exponential point-counting formula
notes: \(Z=\exp(\sum_eN_et^e/e)\), with \(N_e\) the number of homomorphisms \(A\to\mathbb F_{p^e}\); integrality is less obvious in this form.
statement: For finite-type \(X/\mathbb F_q\), \(N_r=\#X(\mathbb F_{q^r})\) and \(Z(X,t)=\exp(\sum_{r\ge1}N_rt^r/r)\). Taking formal logarithms of the Euler product proves the identity through \(N_r=\sum_{d\mid r}db_d\). Integral coefficients follow directly from the Euler product; arbitrary integer sequences \(N_r\) do not automatically give integral exponential coefficients.
reconstruction: The divisibility relation with closed-point counts explains both the logarithm and the integrality caveat.
fate: This identity is the starting formula in \citet[\S1]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Spec Z and the usual Riemann zeta function
notes: Applying the construction to \(A=\mathbb Z\) gives the usual zeta function.
statement: For \(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z\), the norm of the closed point \((p)\) is \(p\), and its arithmetic zeta function is \(\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}=\zeta(s)\) for \(\Re s>1\). There is no single finite base field and hence no common integer degree producing this product in one formal variable \(t\). The analogy uses residue-field norms.
reconstruction: Norms and the complex convergence half-plane replace the finite-field degree variable.
fate: The assertion is a classical Euler-product analogy, not an application of Dwork rationality to the Riemann zeta function \citep[Introduction]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The Borel–Dwork rationality criterion needs compatible radii
notes: The integral-coefficient series converges in a complex disc and is meromorphic p-adically; therefore it is automatically rational.
statement: Let \(F(t)\in\mathbb Z[[t]]\). Suppose it is holomorphic in the complex disc \(|t|<R\) and represents a quotient of convergent power series on the \(\mathbb C_p\)-disc \(|t|_p<r\), with \(|p|_p=p^{-1}\) and \(Rr>1\). Then \(F\in\mathbb Q(t)\). Small positive convergence radii in both norms alone do not suffice; p-adic meromorphy on arbitrarily large discs does suffice once the complex radius is positive.
reconstruction: The crucial inequality between radii, the integral coefficient condition, and the meaning of meromorphic are restored.
fate: Exact pre-talk source: \citet[\S4, Theorem~2; Russian translation p.~68]{dwork1960rationality}. A modern exposition states a slightly broader meromorphic-complex version \citep[Theorem~6.8]{thorne2010padic}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The p-adic valuation ring, residue field, and convergence criterion
notes: \(\mathbb Z_p=\{|x|_p\le1\}\), \(M_p=\{|x|_p<1\}\), residue field \(\mathbb F_p\); \(\sum x_n\) converges iff \(x_n\to0\). Banach spaces carry over.
statement: The valuation ring of \(\mathbb Q_p\) is \(\mathbb Z_p\), its maximal ideal is \(p\mathbb Z_p\), and its residue field is \(\mathbb F_p\). In any complete ultrametric normed vector space a series converges if and only if its terms tend to zero: the ultrametric triangle inequality bounds each finite tail by its largest term. A non-Archimedean Banach space is a complete normed vector space whose norm satisfies that inequality.
reconstruction: Completeness is essential for the implication from vanishing terms to convergence.
fate: The coefficient-field and Banach conventions appear in \citet[\S1]{serre1962endomorphismes}; these are older basic facts.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Completely continuous operators and p-adic Fredholm determinants
notes: In a Banach space a completely continuous operator is nuclear, hence \(\det(1-tA)\) is an entire p-adic function.
statement: Let \(K\) be a complete nontrivially valued non-Archimedean field and let \(E\) be an orthonormalizable Banach space, isomorphic to \(c_0(I,K)\). If \(A\) is a norm limit of finite-rank operators, its Fredholm determinant is well defined by finite-rank approximation and is an entire power series in \(t\). For \(K\) discretely valued, equivalent norms reduce general Banach spaces to this setting. Nuclear is used in Serre\textquoteright s non-Archimedean sense, not the real/complex trace-class condition.
reconstruction: The coefficient field, complete-continuity convention, and orthonormalizability are explicit.
fate: Precisely \citet[\S\S4--5, Proposition~7]{serre1962endomorphismes}; received 18 December 1961 and published in 1962.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: C_p and Teichmüller representatives
notes: \(\Omega\) is the completion of the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q_p\); its valuation ring modulo the maximal ideal is \(F\), and \(F^*\to Z_\Omega^*\) has canonical representatives.
statement: Write \(\mathbb C_p=\widehat{\overline{\mathbb Q}_p}\). Its valuation ring has residue field \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\). If \(a\in\mathbb F_{p^m}^*\), its Teichm\"uller lift is the unique \((p^m-1)\)-st root of unity reducing to \(a\). These lifts are compatible in finite subfields and give a multiplicative section \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p^*\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb C_p}^*\), extended by \([0]=0\). The section is generally not additive.
reconstruction: The completion is metric, the residue field is identified, and multiplicative is distinguished from a ring section.
fate: The field and root-of-unity lifts are part of the p-adic construction in \citet[\S\S1--2]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Nonzero entire p-adic functions have finitely many zeros on bounded discs
notes: An entire series \(\sum c_kt^k\), with coefficients tending sufficiently fast to zero, has finitely many zeros in every finite-radius disc; Shnirelman, maximum principle, Schwarz lemma.
statement: Over \(\mathbb C_p\), an entire power series satisfies \(|c_k|_pR^k\to0\) for every real \(R>0\). If it is not identically zero, it has only finitely many zeros, counted with multiplicity, in every closed disc of finite radius. This follows by the non-Archimedean Weierstrass/Newton-polygon argument, not from topological compactness of the disc.
reconstruction: The coefficient growth, nonzero condition, and closed-disc interpretation are made explicit.
fate: \citet[\S4, Propositions~1--3 and the Shnirelman discussion]{dwork1960rationality} records the analytic facts used in rationality. The notebook omits the exclusion of the zero function.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: The unit ball in Q_p is compact
notes: The unit disc in \(\mathbb Q_p\) is not compact.
statement: The closed unit ball \(\mathbb Z_p\subset\mathbb Q_p\) is compact: it is complete and has a finite covering by residue classes modulo \(p^n\) at every scale. The closed unit ball of \(\mathbb C_p\) is not compact, because its infinite residue field yields infinitely many pairwise distance-one points. Thus \(\mathbb C_p\), the preceding field \(\Omega\), may have been intended, but the scan writes \(\mathbb Q_p\).
reconstruction: The possible intended field is flagged rather than silently substituted.
fate: The valuation-field distinction is standard background \citep[\S1]{serre1962endomorphismes}; the elementary covering argument directly settles the literal statement.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Integral power-series coefficients force integral reciprocal roots in reduced form
notes: \(F(z)=\prod(1-\alpha_i z)/\prod(1-\beta_jz)=1+\sum c_kz^k\), \(c_k\in\mathbb Z\); algebraic \(\alpha_i,\beta_j\) must be algebraic integers.
statement: If \(F\in\mathbb Q(z)\cap(1+z\mathbb Z[[z]])\) is expressed as a reduced quotient, normalized with numerator and denominator constant terms one, then every reciprocal zero and reciprocal pole is an algebraic integer. Indeed both \(F\) and its formal inverse have p-adically integral coefficients; neither can have a zero or pole at \(|z|_p<1\). Apply this at every algebraic embedding and every prime. Cancellation must be removed: \((1-z/2)/(1-z/2)=1\) is an immediate counterexample without that condition.
reconstruction: Reducedness, normalization, and the inverse-series argument supply the missing hypotheses and handle numerator zeros as well as poles.
fate: The notebook\textquoteright s valuation argument is made complete here; it is classical arithmetic of rational integral series, consistent with the integrality framework of \citet[\S4]{dwork1960rationality}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established mathematics predating this talk; the qualification in the statement is essential.

title: Hyperbolic orbit counting and the leading asymptotic
notes: Integer points are preimages on the universal cover; the count is area plus a term proportional to boundary length, both of the same order.
statement: Let \(M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^2\) be a compact hyperbolic surface of curvature \(-1\), with \(\Gamma\) torsion free, and fix \(z,w\in\mathbb H^2\). Then \(N_\Gamma(R;z,w)=\#\{\gamma\in\Gamma:d(z,\gamma w)\le R\}\sim\pi e^R/\operatorname{area}(M)\), equivalently \(N_\Gamma(R;z,w)\sim\operatorname{area}(B_R)/\operatorname{area}(M)\). Here \(\operatorname{area}(B_R)=2\pi(\cosh R-1)\) and \(\operatorname{length}(\partial B_R)=2\pi\sinh R\); both grow like \(\pi e^R\).
reconstruction: Compactness, curvature, lattice normalization, and the constant are supplied. No independent lower-order boundary term is inferred from two quantities of the same exponential order.
fate: \citet[Theorems~1--2]{margulis1969applications}, received 6 June 1969 and published later that year, establishes the leading asymptotic and its constant. It does not provide the notebook\textquoteright s unspecified two-term area-plus-boundary formula.
present_status: As of November 2026: the identified result is established, with the scope stated here.

title: The square-root remainder and the hyperbolic circle problem
notes: The remainder is of the order of the square root of the first terms. Neither coefficients nor a precise error expression are written.
statement: The precise modern question reconstructed here is the pointwise hyperbolic circle problem. For a fixed cofinite Fuchsian group and fixed points, subtract the full spectral main term, including contributions from Laplace eigenvalues below \(1/4\). Is the remaining error \(O_{\varepsilon,\Gamma,z,w}(X^{1/2+\varepsilon})\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), where \(X\asymp e^R\)? This is weaker than a literal uniform \(O(e^{R/2})\) claim and more specific than the notebook\textquoteright s unspecified first terms.
reconstruction: The group class, pointwise quantifiers, spectral subtraction, and epsilon loss are explicit modern additions. The notebook itself does not state this fully qualified conjecture.
fate: \citet[Theorem~6]{margulis1969applications} distinguishes the count from complementary-series contributions. The later standard conjecture and the classical \(O(X^{2/3})\) barrier are stated in \citet[Introduction, equations~(1.3)--(1.4)]{chatzakosetal2025hyperbolic}, first posted 16 June 2025. Their Theorem~1.1 improves the error only for specified Heegner points; it does not solve the general pointwise problem. \citet[Theorems~1.1--1.2]{biro2026localsquare}, first posted 13 April 2026, studies a local \(L^2\) average and a conditional improvement of its exponent; it does not settle the pointwise conjecture.
present_status: As of November 2026: the reconstructed general pointwise \(X^{1/2+\varepsilon}\) bound remains open in the searched primary literature. The 2025 special-point logarithmic saving and the 2026 local-mean conditional improvement are different partial results \citep[Introduction and Theorem~1.1]{chatzakosetal2025hyperbolic}\citep[\S1.1]{biro2026localsquare}. The original unspecified \(O(e^{R/2})\) announcement is not verified.
worth: Worth developing now: separating the main spectral terms from the remainder exposes the exact obstruction to reading the notebook as a proved square-root bound.

title: Horocycle ergodicity in counting
notes: Ergodicity of the horospherical flow is used in an important way.
statement: For compact negatively curved manifolds, the geodesic flow has stable and unstable horospherical foliations. Suitable transverse or leafwise measures and their asymptotic invariance allow one to relate dynamical equidistribution to counts in the universal cover. This explains the counting method without asserting that bare ergodicity alone supplies a quantitative error rate.
reconstruction: The published measure construction is distinguished from an effective mixing estimate, which would be needed for a specific remainder.
fate: \citet[Theorem~5 and Remark~6]{margulis1969applications} explicitly says that the horospherical measure construction is used to prove the counting theorems; received June 1969, published 1969.
present_status: As of November 2026: the identified result is established, with the scope stated here.

title: The analogy with Linnik’s integer points on spheres
notes: Linnik has work on how many points lie on a sphere.
statement: The notice connects homogeneous dynamics with arithmetic lattice-point problems. It does not specify a radius sequence, congruence restriction, counting theorem, or equidistribution claim, and does not state that the hyperbolic and Euclidean spherical problems have identical errors.
reconstruction: Only the explicit analogy is retained; no theorem from Linnik\textquoteright s broader work is imported.
fate: This is a thematic return to the earlier Linnik discussion indexed as 1964-14.2. The current line is too short to identify an additional precise result or recurring problem.
